WE are informed by DODD'S Parliamentary
Companion that CIIABLES JOIIN Er. Ewen' is
Bishop of Gloucester and Bristol, that he has
sat in the House of Lords since 1864, that he
is patron of seventy livings, and that his in-
come—without "perquisites "—is £5,000 per
annum. We take it for granted, therefore,
that said CIIAULES JOIN ELLICOTT is a com-
fortable man, devoted to the Church, and upon
the whole rather pleased than otherwise with
the existing state of things. It is not certain he
will leave the Church to join any one of our
dissenting bodies, or that he will sympathise
with any form of political discontent, or en-
courage in any way grumbling against autho-
rity iu any, department of the State. CIIARLES
JonN tuicoTT;would be simply a fool if he
did, and whatever else this exalted and pious
person may, be, he is certainly not. simple
enough to quarrel with his bread and butter,
especially as it is so nicely and :so plentifully
buttered on both sides.

But then it must not be forgotten that
CHARLES JOHN ELLICOTT is Bishop in a
Christian Church a rich Church, estab-
lished in one of the wealthiest countries in
the world; nor ought it to be necessary to re-
call the fact that the doctrines of this Church
teach humility to the exalted and powerful;
justice and kindly consideration to till ; and
that the founders of the Christian religion, of
which our English Church is presumed to be
one of the purest forms, wore poor needy men,
"agitators" who did not own one acre of
land; who did not sit in high places at the
feasts of the landowners of Judea; but who
rather hungered on the highways, glad to
feast on green figs as they journeyed between
Bethany and Jerusalem.

It would not be fair to ask CITIRLES JOHN
.ELLicorr to do as these did. Ile is under no
necessity to trudge on foot through his diocese
with an umbrella under his arm. We do not
desire that he should be called on to bear im-
prisonment or stripes. He has been born into
better times than those in which the Apostles
lived, and there is no reason on earth why he
should not enjoy them ;nay more, if CIRRI:VS
JOHN ELLICOTT, like most of his Episcopal
brethren, can reconcile it to his conscience to
slink aside; and leave those great duties of
humanity unperformed, which may be con-
sidered as naturally belonging to his office,
nobody would think of being too severe on
him for a sin which he shares in common with
'nearly every dignitary in the Church to which
he belongs. -

PATERNAL LEGISLATION.

"SIIL JOAN LUBBOCK hit one of the greatest
wants of the day when he enacted holidays by
statute. The force of competition rendered it
too great a risk to forego opportunities of
trade, of which advantage might be taken by
a more industrious rival, and nothing but a
statute could have broken the spell."

, The above passage I take from a leading
article, of yesterday's (the 6th inst.) Times. I
do not quote it for ,the purpose of denying the
proposition it contains, but merely in order to
point out the readinessavith which certain classes
avail themselves of that" paternal legislation" -
which their representatives, both in Parlia-
ment and in the press, are constantly denounc-
ing as a dangerous snare when it is invoked
on behalf of working men. Where was Mr.
FANCETT when, Sir JOHN LlTBDOCX.proposed to
treat commercial men like children by the
" paternal " intervention of the State? We
know very 'Well that if a piece of prohibitory •
legislation had been demanded in the interest
•. of the working classes—whether for the pur-
pose of preventing helpless miners from being
swindled by their masters, or for the pur-
pose of providing gratuitous edueation for
the helpless children of helpless parents or
if a proposal had been before the, House'
to tax the wealth iastead of the poverty
of the -nation, that Mr. FawcEtt- would
, have been in his place, to declaim, with the
rare courage of his convictions, as the phrase
goes,upon the danger of paternal legislation, and
the demoralizing tendency of workmen to seek
the protection of the State. What would
. have beau said. by the HERBERT SPENCER,
SChOOl of Political Economists if a Bill had
been introduced to Parliament with the object
of crating a holiday by statute for the work-
ing classes every twentieth Tuesday? We
know perfectly well that such a proposal would
have been howled down amid universal ridicule.
What homilies we should have had upon "over
legislation" of soeialistio theories. Yet a
similar proposal is brought forward on behalf
of the represented classes, and it is passed with
acclamation, while the leading upper and
middle class 'argon 'inform aa that by means of
it the "greatest want of the day" is
satisfied. ..

Working clam pliticians need to be on 'their
guard. They must not allow themselves to be
imposed upon by pretensions or delusive
phrases. Their opponents have ever been
ingeniou4 in affixing a stigma by means of an
epithet; and the curious and disheartening fact
Is that working men, in their simplicity, have
been too frequently led to distrust their
best friends ur moat powerful loaders 9a

account of a missile flung by political
antagonists. For centuries the term
" demagogue " has been successfully used
as a scarecrow, frightening working men, and
carrying confusion in their ranks; and yet
it may be said that no true proletariate leader
has ever appeared without receiving the brand
of "demagogue." In the same way "paternal
legislation" is used as a bugbear to intimi-
date workmen from exercising legislative
power in the interest of their class. Let them
exercise their intelligence and perceive that
legislation is now termed " paternal " when-
ever it is favourable to their order. The
phrase is convenient and opportune. Hitherto
legislation has been the exclusive privilege of
the upper and middle classes, and it has been
unscrupulously exercised on their behalf:
consequently, notwithstanding the piles of
statutes which have been accumulating for
centuries, we have never heard any remon-
strance about " paternal" legislation. Now,
however, that legislative form is passing from
their hands into those of the labouring class,
the convenient discovery is made that all
legislation is useless, and the laissez faire
economist becomes the darling of both parties.
Mons. BARTIAT'S theory, that there is no such
thing as a State at all, becomes exceedingly
popular; the collective power of society to
improve the circumstances which create
3,000,000
.paupers per annum is vehemently
denied; the pauper and the pauper's child,
notwithstanding a surrounding monopoly of
the moans of livelihood, has the regenerating
means at his own oommand ; let him enter
the divine competitive struggle, and if he fails

starve, the "divinely appointed penalty of

doctrine greedily adopted by the Conservatives

Radicals. The quotation I have given from

its true character. Legislation which benefits
the House of 'Commons class is " sound,"

MAZZINI ON THE SOCIAL QUESTION.
TUE remarks of MAzzirtr on the SJoial
Question, quoted in the Bxe-HIVE of July 20,
are applicable to the subject as he viewed it,
and as it is viewed by those who do not under-
stand it. Political and aocial reformers who
have not acquired the knowledge of the
causes of evil and of good, in the for-
Bastion of character, in the production
and distribution Of wealth, and in
social affairs generally, and who, therefore,
however good their intentions may be, can-
not have acquired the enlightened goodwill
to all which this knowledge alone can produce,
cannot understand "the social question."
Their ideas of the reforms which are re iuired
for the establishment of justice among men,
and for the fulfilment by all men of the duty
of doing to others as we, would have others to
do to us, must be extremely limited, and there-
fore their desires and aspirations must be ex-
tremely limited. They cannot, therefore, have
any
.ideas of the institution by which alone
a system of justice and good will to all can be
realised, and of course they cannot have any
idea of the means by which alone these insti-
tutions can be established.
The reformer who understands these sub-
jects sees and feels that a general equality of
education, and equality of condition according
to age, are necessary for justice to all; and
anything short of this must be unsatisfactory
to him, as inconsistent with enlightened good
will to all and with enlightened ideas of
'justice. And he knows that wider arrange-
ments in which the production and distribu-
tion of wealth will be well regulated, the
supply of wealth for all will be so abundant,
that the private posscssion of it, except such
as is perfectly compatible with justice and
with kind feelings towards all, will be as use-
less as water bottled up would be when there
is always a plentiful supply of fresh water to
be easily obtained.
And men who have acquired the character
of the new system will not desire to have any
social privileges, while similar wiyintagek

are not equally attainable by all, according to
age; and they will know and feel that
inequalities of educational advantages, and of
condition according to age, are causes of evil

those who have less advantages than others.
But reformers must be better taught than
they have hitherto been, before they call
reasonably be expected to be better in-

Property, MazziNr says, is an "eternal prin-

MAZZINI speaks of the intellectual and moral

And while they are thus ignorant, the di
culties to which he refers with respect to

must appear insurmountable. And they will
be insurmountable while men continue to be
intellectually and, morally what they have
hitherto been. When men have a,oquired
the character of the new system—when they
understand its arrangements, and when they •
have the ideas and feelings of which

appear. _

Of course I do not defend any views of the
"social question" which are not based upon
the improved formation of character of the •
new system. such views can only be the
unpractical and impracticable ideas of men
who desire the correction of the glaringly,
unjust, and injurious institutions of the
psesent system, but who have not the know-
ledge, and cannot, therefore, have the cha-
racter, necessary to enable men to remedy
these evils effectually, and in the spirit of good
will to all.

To facilitate the study of this great subjeot,
I have just published a cheap tract, "The
Coming Revolution," in which the leading
points of it are briefly, and, I think, plainly
stated. (See advertisement.)

The following is the continuation of the article

The remedy for your condition cannot be found
in general, arbitrary organizations built up by one
or another intellect, contradicting the universal

and always will be, rebellious towards designs of

An increase in wages fixed by the governing

instrumental cause of labour and of production
The remedy forsour condition lies in the union of
capital and labour in the same hands.
When society knows no distinction, save that

law of fixed wages.

Associated labour, the division of the fruits of
labour, or of the proceeds of the sal t of these;

the social future. In this lies the senret of your

OLDHAM.
TUE BUILDERS' STRIKE.

An aggregate meeting of carpenters and Joiners
was held on Monday evening, July 29, at the
White Bear Inn, Oldham, for the purpose of
meeting Messrs. Benny and Burgess, the deputation
sent down to address their Lancashire brethren.
Mr. T. Bleasdale presided.
The Chairman, in opening the mooting, ex-
pressed the pleasure he felt at meeting with two
such thorough-going trades unionists as Messrs.
Denney and Burgess, and said ho felt confident
that when the Lancashire men had heard the
statements of the deputation they would readily
sad nobly respond to the request for assistance.
He then called upon Mr. Bonney to address the
meeting.
Mr. Benny gave a detailed account of the nine
hours movement from the commencement up to
the present time. He said that although the
London men were te first to agitate for the nine
hours, it appeared as if they were going to be the
last in obtaining it. He strongly denounced the
,conduct of Mr. Broadhurst and the stonemasons
for going to work without consulting the carpen-
ters and joiners, as he thought they ought to have
been informed of their intentions, as they had
been working for ono common cause. He con-
cluded a spirited address by appealing to those
present to consider their case. -

Mr. Burgess delivered a long and interesting
address on capital and labour,* and clearly showed
that the profits derived from the latter were very
unequally divided, He concluded by earnestly
requesting the men in Oldham to assist the car.
penters and joiners in London in their endeavours
to obtain a satisfactory code of working rules.
It was ilea proposed, seconded, and carried
unanimously—
That we pledge ourselves to pay a subscription
of sixpence per week per man so long its the strike
continues,

A. committee vras then elected to carry out the
foregoing resolution.

A vote of thanks was given to -the deputation
for the able addressee they' had delivered.
A vote of thanks to the chairman concluded the
meeting.

BIRKENHEAD.
TILE SHIPBUILDERS' STRIKE.

The strike amongst the men in the employ of
Messrs. Laird. Brothers, engineers and shipbuilders,
Birkenhead, still continues, and the men decline
to return to work on anything but their full
demand of 10 per cent, increase on their present
wages.

At the last meeting of the men, on Friday
night, a communication was read from the em-
ployers, stating that they considered an advance
of 2s. a week which they had offered to the men
a fair and reasonable one, and would consequently
adhere to it. Some of the men were inclined to
accept the offer, but on being Put to the vote it
was decided by a large majority to accept no other
terms than the original demand of 10 per cent.
increase. Up to the present thnstrike continues,
and there appears at present to be no liktlihood of
any final agreement. , • .

if necessary by their subscriptions—was therefore
happily a resumption of work on Monday morning
by the whole of the 700 men who have been so long

articles.title: LONDON CARPENTERS'
articles.text:
THE LONDON CARPENTERS'

STRIKE.

Th. adjournment of the Master Builders'
Committee for a month and the resolutions of the
carpenters' delegates to fall back upon the terms
of the memorial, and to withdraw the offer made
to the masters and rejected by them on Wednes-
day, have destroyed all probability of any early
settlement of the dispute. The Central Com-
mittee of the carpenters held a meeting on
Monday to consider the moet elliiient manner
in which the stiuggle could be carried on, and
several plans and suggestions were brought
forward having that object in view. Some of
these plans were at once rejected as impractie
able, however desirable they might be, while
others, which appeared to be of a more practical
character, were referred to a sub-committee to
report upon previous to taking into counsel the
various district committees. In the meantime,
the vigilance committees in each district were
instructed to u,e every legitimate effort to draw
out all men working for the closed firms, and to
place them upon the strike fund where necessary.
Fresh appeals were ordered to be made to the
trades throughout the country, informing them
of the existing state of affairs, and notices were
forwarded to all the large towns, warning car-
penters and joiners to keep_ away from London
during the existence of the present dispute.

At the present time the pasition isthis. There
are 53 building firms for whom carpenters and
joiners aro prohibited by the delegates flora work-
ing, in consequence of their having taken part in
late lock-ou in opposition to the terms of

memorial. The number of joiners now on strike
against these firms is about 1,600, the numbers
a few weeks since having been about 2,000, but
reduced by the men having obtained employment
at other firms either in London or the provinces.
Within the last fortnight some of the above firms
have succeeded in obtaining men, and with this
limited staff manage to execute their most pressing
work. Some of these firms have also received
material assistance from what are called
"machinists," or "machine joiners," several of
whom have accepted the offer of led. and lid.
per hour. These facts, although they might have
no ultimate effect upon the result of the strike,
may cause it to "drag its slow length along," and
have necessitated some change in the position.
On Monday, the men on strike from Jackson and
Shaw's and Brass's were paid their ninth dividend
at the rate of 14s. per week each, and the others
their sixth, at the rate of II s. per week each, or
is. less in each case than last week.

On Thursday morning the Carpenters' Com-
mittee received letters from their deputations in
Yorkshire and Lancashire of a most satisfactory
and an encouraging character. A largo amount in
Post-office orders from the country were also re-
ceived, and the finance committee are sanguine of
being able to pay a 15s. dividend to the men on
Monday next. A number more men have been
drawn up, and some of the firms who
have succeeded, after a good deal of trouble and
expense, in obtaining men from distant parts—
and in the West of England especially—now find
their shops again empty. Notwithstanding the
fact that at least two-thirds of the men who
originally struck work have either been absorbed
in the shops of the small masters or gone to
country jobs; the number of men on the strike
fund remain at about 2,000, owing to the largo
number of men who have been drawn out from the
closed firms.

THE LONDON HOUSE PAINTERS.

A large meeting of house painters, chiefly of the
firm of Messrs. Waller, was held on Saturday

purpose of considering what course should be
adopted by the trade in consequence of the masters
having refused to accede to the teims of the
memorial lately sent in by the men for a reduction
of the hours of labour to 61 hours per week,
and the minimum rate of wages to be sid. per.
hour.

The chairman, in opening the proceedings, said
that the present meeting had been called to receive
a report of a deputation who had been asked to
wait upon the Painters' Central Committee to
seek their advice as to the course to be pursued in
consequence of the masters having broken faith
with the men in leading them to understand
that there should be a uniform rate of wages and
working hours throughout the trade.
Mr. Shipton said the question now before
them to deoide was whether they were pre-
pared to strike or not. If the men of
Messrs. Waller's firm were prepared to come out,
he was prepared to tell them that the Central
Committeo of the Trade was prepared to 8 I:pport
them. '1 ho committee were in a position to give
them a certain amount Per week to staTt with,
and as soon as they were out he had no doubt the
funds for their farther support would come in.
What he would advise them to do was to co:ne
to some decisiop at once, whether they would
come out or not; and then if they chose to do so,
to pass a resolution placing themselves in the
hands of the Central Committee. The Central
Committee would then write to Messrs. Waller at
once, give them a certain time to reply in, and if
no reply came in a few days, would call the
whole of the men out.

A workman suggested that'the question of time
should be entirely left alone till next March.
After some discussion, the following resolution
was put to the meeting, Messrs. Waller's men
only being allowed to vote upon it :

That this meeting of Messrs. Wallets men
express their willingness to place themselves in the
hands of the Central Committee of 'Painters, and
pledge themselves to cease work when it is

prepared, if necessary, to come out, if called upon,
in support of tNe terms of the memorial—viz.,

ing rules. The secretary was instructed to write
a lettoe to Mr. Waller, asking him to concede the

articles.title: LONDON BAKERS.
articles.text:
THE LONDON BAKERS.

On Saturday evening last, a crowded meeting
of journeymen and operative bakers was held at
the No. 8 branch of the London Union of Opera-
tive Bakers, Darwon-itreet, Old Kent-road, for
the purpose of considering the present position of
the baking trade and the best means to be pursued
with regard to the agitation for a reduction of the
hours of labour now occurring in various parts of
London. Mr. J. Sabine, who was voted to the
chair, said, that up to the present the bakers of
London had been content to be in a worse condition,
earning less wages and working more hours, than
almost any other trade. Now, he was happy to
see that they, as well as others, were on the move,
and he had no doubt their demands, which were
only just and reasonable, would be conceded to
them. With regard to the time of going in to
work in the morning he heard the East-end
German bakers had given the masters notice of a
strike, in the event of non-compliance with their
demands, and had fixed 5 o'clock as the hour to
commence work, but he thought that 4 o'clock
was the more reasonable time, and no consistent*
baker would object to that. He concluded by
assuring the meeting of his own determination to
continue the agitation, and exhorting them to do
the same. Ile also reminded them that the master
bakers of London were anxiously awaiting the
decision of the men generally, and exhorted them
to be just in their demands.

In the course of the evening, reports were read
from the Central Board of the London Union, the
exact terms of which were not procurable, but
which mentioned the subject pf arbitration, and
proposed that 12 influential journeymen should
meet 12 masters on an open and public, platfoini,
there to decide the question with respect to the
bakers' grievances generally. It was also stated
that it was the wish of the majority of the
masters that 4 o'clock should be the time for
beginning work in the morning, which would of
course abolish night work—the great object of the
present agitation.
The demands of the great body of the men
may be stated briefly as follows :—Tho total
abolition of night work, a slight rise of wages,
and the total abolition of Sunday labour. Ott the
last point the feeling of the men is very strong.
The reports from the Central Board were adopted,
and, after other speeches, a vote of thanks to the
chairman concluded the meeting.

THE POSTAL AND TELEGRAPH
SERVICE..

ANOTHER GREAT MEETING OE POSTMEN IN THE

CITY.

On Wednesday morning a meeting of postmen
was held in their kitchen (by permission) to receive
the report of the delegates appointed to wait on
the Postmaster-General. W. Booth, letter-carrier,
was elected to the chair. The chairman impressed
on them the necessity of maintaining a strict guard
over their feelings, and not by any act of theirs
give cause for complaint. He said he hoped
that if they were satisfied with the answer given
to their petition they would express such feeling;
if the contrary, by the resolution they passed they
should express their opinion emphatically, unmis-
takably, yet deferentially :and, respectfully. Let
not any one counsel a resort to violent action by
any moans, as the justness of their cause would
bear a searching inquiry, and undergo the test
satisfactorily. Of that he was convinced. There
were two sides to every question; the one, the
economically official one of the employers; the
reverse—viz., a fair day's work and a fair day's
pay, with a defined rule of promotion laid down
for the employed. Unless there was some prospect
of improving the position of the employed, dis-
satisfaction would always exist, more or less, in
accordance with the amount of pay received.
Promotion as at present carried out offered none or
but little inducement for exertion of ability. It
gave no stimulant to work, for that he believed
was the general complaint, silent but none the
less deep. The deputation had been complimented
on their ability and the clearness with which
their spokesman had opened their case. He said,
would they be prepared to abide by the argument
as laid down by the Postmaster-General—viz.,
that if they increased the wages of civil servants
when the price of articles of daily necessity in-
creased, so also ought they to reduce them when
prices fell—would they accept this, so that as
prices had risen 30 per cent, since the last revision
of their salaries, they should have their wages
increased 30 per cent., with the understanding
that when prices fell their wages should be re-
duced accordingly ? (Loud cries of " Yes.")
.Again, if justice were impattially administered
according to that argument, the same thing would
apply with respect to the profits made out of the
labour of 'the employes. Would they accept that
as being correct? (" Yes, yes.") And now for
the last, were they satisfied with the "revised
scale" as an answer to their petition? (An
universal cry of "No.") He now called upon
their delegates to make their statement, which
was to the effect already'publishod In the papers,
they also saying that, owing to the pressure of
time, the Postmaster-General had, been unable to
hear any reply they might have wished to make
to his remarks. (" Shame,", "As usual," and
other not very complimentary remarks.) The
chairman having called the meeting to order, the
delegates continued, and said:they had done their
best and could do no more. Their mission being
accomplished they Inw resigned their office.
The thanks of the meeting were unanimously
accorded them. The chairman said that they had
heard the toport of Weir delegates, Messrs. Wood
and- Sirett, and he would again ask the question
were they satisfied with the answer to their
petition? ("No, no! ") He took each clause
separately to ascertain on which points they were
satisfied or dissatisfied. Did they think that, con-
sidering the net profits of ~the Poet Office, after
payment.of all expenses, had increased nearly one
million in the last ten years, that their pay should
be increased accordingly ? (Cries of " Yes, yes !"
"We mean to have it, too.") lie hoped that
expression would not be repeatod. After each
clause of the petition and the Postmaster-General's
reply thereto had been discussed, the following
resolution was unanimously carried amid the
utmost enthusiasm, the meeting pledging them-
selyes to support it by every means in their power,
it also being denied that the wages of a letter-
carrier were so high as made out by the authorities,
except in certain individual cases. The pro-
posal to give stripes for good conduct was con-
demned by all, and stigmatised as an insult to'those
whose conduct should in all cases be good, otherwise
they should rot be retained in the service; and
hopes were expressed that it would not be carried
out, as it would only give rise to increased agita-
tion to abolish them. It was proposed by Mr.
letter-carrier, and emended by Mr.
Twelvetrees, letter-carrier—

That this meeting of the East Central District
letter-carriers, having heard the report of the
de:egates appointed by them to wait on the Postmaster
General, and while grateful to that gentleman for
bis kindness in receiving them, and for any
benefit afforded by the "Revised Scale," still
consider the same an unsatisfactory anwer to their
petition of March 5, 1872, and hereby elect Mr.
Berry, letter-carrier, and Mr. H. Bailey, letter-
carrier, as their representatives to act on a corn-

mittee to prepare a petition, either to the Lords of
the Treasury or to Parliament, praying for an
i improvement n their position, or a Parliamentary
inquiry, or otherwise to act as circumstances may
demand. The said committeb to have full power,
as representing their constituents, to sign all
applications and petitions.

MEETING or LOCAOHIRE COLLIURS.

On Monday a meeting of miners and delegates
of the Bolton, Rochdale, and Bury district was
held at the Church Hotel, Kersley, under the
presidency of Mr. J. Worrell. Upwards of 2,000
miners were represented. Mr. T. Halliday, pre-
sident of the Amalgamated Association, addressed
the meeting upon the wages and short time move-
ment. lie stated that within tho labt month the
colliery proprietors had put an advance of 2. Gd.
per ton on coal, and he contended that the miners
had a right to a Mr share of that. advance—
namely, 30 per cent. At Wigan and other places,
it was said the men were asking for an additional
30 per cent., which he could not but think was a
mistake. (A. voice: "It's no mistake.") Well,
then, he hoped they would get it; but the masters
had decided not to give any advance until after
the first making-up day in October, and then it
was to be only 10 per cent. Wages had increased
in Staffordshire and other parts of the country,
but notwithstanding this, be contended that the
miners had not received an advance proportionate
to the profits of the ;nesters. With regard to the
eight hours moveramt, he regretted that the
Clifton Colliery Company and the firm of Messrs.
.4.. Knowles and Sons were not working short time;
but he was afraid that the men were. as much to
blame as the employers, and if they would not join
the union they must put up with what they had
to contend with. A. resolution was proposed and
seconded that 16 per cent. more be demanded from
the employers; but to this an amendment was
moved that the- masters should be requested to
meet the men, and consult as to the disproportion
in the wages paid to the men and the advance put
upon the price of coal. On a division, the amend-
ment was carried by 21 against six.

A struggle between masters and men in the
South Staffordshire coal trade has for the present
been avetted. The compromise of Mr. Fisher
Smith, the representative of the Earl of Dudley,
who is also chairman of the United Association of
Staffordshire Masters, has now been adopted
by the other masters east and west of Dudley,
and the leaders of the men have succeeded in in-
ducing most of the men to resume work. It was
found that the funds of the two local unions wore
not in a state to justify a strike, and Mr. Halli-
day, the chairman of the National Amalgamation
of Miners; Mr. Pickard, of Cannock Chase ; Mr.
Gethin, agent of the South Staffordshire Union ;
Mr. Griffiths, of West Bromwich, and other pro-
minent leaders of the men, spoke at a great meet-
ing at Willenhall on Friday night. At this same
place 2,000 men had two nights before rejected
the masters' proposition come to at the Wolver-
hampton meeting. They now, however, accepted
the compromise, and, acting upon the advice of
their leaders, went to work on the following day.
They will not, however, be satisfied unless they
have another 6d. The loaders promised to try to
get them this much more a Clay by inteiviewing
the masters, and consented that, if it could not be
got in this way, notice Should be given for it next
Saturday. In the localities where the men remain
out, they assert they will endure any amount of
privation before-they yield.

NOV= WEOT LA.NCASUIRE MINERS.

The miners' delegates representing the various
districts of South-west Lancashire have decided
to send in 14 days' notice for an advance of 30
per cent. in the rate of wages. The circulars,
which were issued on Monday, state that the men,
after due consicltration of the prosperous condition
of the coal trade, and the higher cost of the neces-
saries of life, think they are entitled to an
increase of pay. There are fears that serious
complications will be the result of these notices,
for only lust week the coal proprietors held a
meeting, and decided to give no increase at pre-
sent, but to grant an advance of 10 per cent. in
October if the state of trade then justified it.

Upwards of 2,000 men employed in the bitu-
minous collieries of the Rhonda, Ely, and Ogmore
Valleys, are now on strike for an advance of
wages. The Steam Coal Colliery Owners' Asso-
elation resolutely supptrts the meters, and has
just passed a resolution prohibiting its members
from," taking on" any of the colliers who have
left work at the bituminous pits. The bulk of
the coal raised by the men on strike is rased for
smelting and coking purposes at the great iron-
works of the district; but about one-third has
been appropriated to domestic use. The result of
the strike has already been a sensible increase in
the price of house coal, and all other classes of
fuel are more or less affected in a similar manner.
Steam coal is now freely realising upwards of 20s.
ton at Cardiff, and there is a general impression

DR. LIVINGSTONE'S LETTER.

We have received from the Foreign-office
copies of the despatches which have been sent
there by Dr. Living-stone. The first is ad-
dressed to Lord Stanley, and is dated as far
back as November 1870. The second and
third are to Lord Clarendon, and bear date a
year later—viz., November 1, 1871. The,
reet are'addressecl to Earl Granville, and range
in date from November 14, 1871, to February
20 of the present year. There is an enclosure
in one of them fur Dr. Kirk. In the last
named communication, which is dated Ujiji,
Oct. 30, 1871, with a postscript of November
16, 1871, Dr. Livingstone complains that his
supplies having been entrusted to slaves were
squandered on the way, be himself getting
scarcely any. lie adds that freemen are abun-
dant at Zanzibar, and that he might wait
twenty years if he had to depend upon slaves.
In the letter to the Earl of Clarendon he says
he has ascertained that the watershed of the
Nile is broad upland between 10 degs. and 12
degs. south latitude, and from 4,000 to 5,000
feet above the level of the sea, with moun-
tains upon it between 6,000 and 7,000 feet in
height. The 'springs that rise on this water-
shed, which is over 700 miles in length from
West to East, are so numerous that it would
take a large part of a man's life to count
them, and a bird's-eye view of some parts
would resemble the "frost vegetation on
window panes."

articles.title: TUE BALLOT ACT.
articles.text:
TUE BALLOT ACT.

The Act to amend the law relating to Parlia-
mentary and Municipal elections has just been
issued. It received the Royal assent on the
18th ultimo. There are 33 sections in the
Statute divided into four parts, and there are
six schedules. The first part relates to the
procedure at Parliamentary elections in Eng-
land, Scotland, and Ireland. In England the
nomination of candidates for a county or
borough is to be in writing, by two registered
electors, as proposer and seconder, and eight
other registered electors assenting to the nomi-
nation, and is to be delivered during the time
appointed for the election to the returning
officer by the candidate himself or his proposer
or seconder. If, at the expiration of one hour
after th,e time appointed for the election' no
more candidates stand nominated than tilere
are vacancies to be filled up, the returning
officer shall forthwith declare the candidates
who may stand to be elected, and return their
names to the Clerk of the Crown in Chancery;
but if at the expiration of such hour more
candidates stand nominated than there are
vacancies to be filled up, the returning officer
shall adjourn the election, and shall take
a poll in the manner in the Act mentioned. A
candidate may, during the time appointed for
the election, but not afterwards, withdraw by
giving a notice to that effect, signed by him, to
the returning officer, provided that the pro-
poser of a candidate nominated in his absence
out of the United Kingdom may withdraw such
candidate by a written notice, signed by him,
and delivered to the returning ofheer, together
with a written declaration of such absence of
the candidate. In ease of the death of a,
candidate the returning officer shall counter-
mand notice of the poll, in the ease of a poll
the votes to be taken by Ballot. The ballot-
paper to show the names of the candidates,
with a number printed on the back, and
attached to it a counterfoil with the same
number printed on the face.
At the time of voting the ballot-paper shall
be marked on both sides with an official
mark and delivered to the voter within the
polling station, and the number of such voter
on the register of voters shall be marked on
the counterfoil, and the voter having secretly
marked his vote on the paper, and folded it up
so as to conceal his vote, shall place it in a
closed box in the presence of the officer pre-
siding at the polling-station after having
shown to him the official mark at the back.
Any ballot-paper whieh has not on its bank
the official mark, or in which votes are given
to more candidates than the voter is entitled
to vote for, or in which anything except the
said number on the back is written or marked
by which the voter can be identified, shall be
void and not counted. After the close of the
poll the ballot-boxes shall be sealed up, so as
to prevent the introduction of additional ballot-
papers, and shall be taken charge of by the
returning officer, and that officer shall, in the
presence of such agents, if any, of the candi-
dates as. may be in attendance, open the ballot-
boxes, and ascertain the result of the poll by
counting the votes given to each candidate,
and shall forthwith declare to be elected the
candidates or candidate to whom the majority
of votes has been given, and return their
names to the Clerk of the Crown in Chincery.
The decision of the returning officer as to any
question arising in respect of any ballot-paper
shall be final, subject to reversal on petition
questioning the election or return. Were an
equality of votes is found to exist between
candidates, and the addition of a vote would
entitle any such candidate to be declared
elected, the returning officer may give such
additional vote, but shall not in any other case
be entitled to vote at an election for which he
is returning officer. The offences in respect
or nomination-papers, ballot-papers, and
ballot-boxes arc set forth. The law is nmended
as to the division of counties and boroughs
into polling districts. The duties of return-
ing officers and the election officers are
detailed. The alterations as to Scotland and
as to Ireland are set forth. The second part
of the Statute relates to municipal elections,
meutary
and the third part to " personation" at Parlia-
and mnnicipal elections. It is to be
deemed a felony, and the offender is to be
liable to two years' itnprisonment with bard
labour.

In the fourth part of the Act the schedules
and notes are to be deemed part of the Act.
The Acts repealed, accordion- to the extent
specified in the schedules. The Statute is to be
'cited as '.‘The Ballot , Act, 1872," and to
continue in force until the 31st of December,
1880, and no longer, unless Parliament shall
otherwise determine.. The first schedule con-
tains rules for Parliamentary plec.tions, the poll,
country votes, "and general provisions. The
second part
.contains roles for municipal elec-
tions. The se,cend schedule contains forms to
be used, and the other schedules relate to the
various statutes effected. by, the new law.
There are six offences set forth at elections.
Every person is guilty of an offence who forges
or fraudulently defapes for fraudulently de-
stroys any nomination-paper, or delivers to the
returning officer any nomination-paper, know-
ing the same to be forged, or forges, or counter-
feits, or fraudulently defaces or fraudulently
destroys any ballot-paper, or the official mark
on any ballot-paper, or without dao authority
supplies any ballot-paper to any person, or
fraudulently puts into any ballot-box any
ballot-paper other than the ballot-paper be is
authorized by law to put in, or .fraudulently
takes out of the polling-station any ballot-
paper, or without due authority destroys,
takes, opens, or otherwise interferes with any
ballot-box or packet of ballot-papers then in
use for the purposes of the election. Any such
offence is to be deemed a misdemeanour, tuad'a
returning
,officer Or clerk in attendance at a
polling-station is to be liable for it to two
years' imprisonment, with or without hard
labour, or any other person to six months'
imprisonment, with or without hard labour.
Any attempt to commit any of the Offendes
specified is to be dealt With in the way of
punishment as the offenee itself is punishable.

SATURDAY, AUGUST 10, 1872.

CARDWELL'S DIEN.

Wu/iv:vim change may be made in any
important branch of the public service, pre-
sumably in Ito interest of the nation, it is
above all things desirable that it should be
carried out in good faith. The army is a very
important branch of the public service. We
are all interested in the way its affairs are
administered, in its discipline and efficiency.
Nobody ever denied that the old method of
officering it was in many respects defective.
Those, however, who were prejudiced in its
favour, or who in any way profited by its

abuses, resisted every attempt to reform it.
We all know haw the Government finally
succeeded in forcing the change, and WO arc
now beginning to find out the spirit in which
those who hold commissions in the service are
opposing the new system.
Lieutenant TRIBE'S case seems to have little
to do with the matter; but in the House of
Commons on Saturday last it brought out the
fact that the officers appointed under the new'
system are marked for contumely and insult,
under the title of " CARDWELL'S men." Al a
matter of course, the public will allow som°.
slight latitude to men acting under a feeling
of irritation, even though thQir insults should
be levelled against those who have had
nothing whatever to do with the changes that
have taken place. But British officers, as a
rule, are supposed to be gentlemen. Loyalty
is their prime duty, and honest service to
their country but an ordinary equivalentsuoh.
as the commonest soldier in the service is sup-
posed to render for that which the country gives
him. In every sense of duty, on every
principle of honour, they are bound to do
nothing by which the efficiency of the service
can be impaired, or the intention of the
Government and the country thwarted.
Union men and non-union men work side
by side in our great industrial establishments
without insulting each other, and if they did
so, injuriously to each other's interests, or to
the injury of their employers, the law would
very soon be brought to bear for the purpose
of reducing them to order. What would not
be allowed in the workshop should not be
tolerated in the barrack. The injury which
would not be permitted in the case of a private
individual should not be countenanced where
the interests of the nation are concerned. If
a spirit of caste or clanship shows itself
amongst the officers of the army, it should be
struck at unsparingly. The change made
must be fairly carried out, and CARDWELL'S
men" treated with as much consideration and
respect as if every one of them had made his
purse the evidence of his fitness for his posi-
tion.

In enforcing the changes decided on, the
working men of the country will support the
Government. Every blow struck at our old
system of caste will meet with a decided
public approval. Let aristocratic airs be
played off where they are no detriment to any
branch of the public service; but where they
operate injuriously they should be treated as
unceremoniously and as severely as if those
who indulged in them were the lowest in the
community. The vulgarity of such a pro-
ceeding might be overlooked, but its evil effect
on so important a branch of the public service
as the army, cannot, under any pretence
whatever, be tolerated. Our officers should
remember that in a few years " CA.RDwELL's
men ",will form a very important portion of
their body, and the fewer insults they may
have to call to mind as incitements to retalia-
tion, the better it will be for everybldy con-
cerned.

but if they have the sense to be instructed by
the lesson it contains, they may•at no very
distant time turn it to profit. Without going
into any argument about the principles of
trades' unionism, or the general utility of
trades' unions for the promotion of working
men's interests, one valuable truth is made
manifest by every struggle that takes place
between working men, and their employers,
which should never be lost sight of. Those
whose destiny it is to live by the labour of
their hands, should shape the policy they
pursue in accordance with their condi-
tion as an organized or an unorganized
body. If a trade has all its members en-
rolled, disciplined, and loyal to each other,
when the circumstances of the case call for it
they can take the field as an army would,
under appointed leaders, provided with a cm-
missaria.t, and all else required, and fight out
the campaign on a fair calculation as to the
consequences of every step taken.

Men so prepared, if they feel called on, may
reasonably enter on war, and may, if they act
prudently and with ordinary pluck, count ow

victory. On the other hand, those not
in union act foolishly when they rush into
action, because, in the very nature of things,
all the chances are against them. Their want
of union is evidence of other unfavourable
conditions, every one of which militates to
their injury. Unskilled men are frequently
not in union because of the large number
which cannot be brought into necessary har-
mony of design and action, and should a
strike take place, the employers can always

take advantage of those not in association
with their fellows. Frequently, too, this
want of associative power is the result of ig-
norance, and the suspicion and distrest
naturally belonging to it. But whatever the
cause, working men so situated resera-
, ble a mob and not a regular army. If
they enter upon a conflict they have no means
of support, no mutual trust, no confidence,
and therefore no patience; in a word, no
• staying power. If they are to win at all they
• must do's° by a sudden rush, and if they fail
in this they sink into the _ condition of a
mere rabble, and have no resource but to yield
and cry out pitiably to their conquerors for
mercy.
This has been the case with the London
and
.North-Western , porters, and in this we
read the usual lesson—not to attempt fighting
without union, and the preparedness union
should always carry with it. With this the
workman may, to a certain extent, make him-
self master of the situation; without it he has
nothing for it but to submit to the unregulated
action of what our political economists call
"demand and supply," and what that means,
under the pressure of competition, the work-
ing men and women of England have had
most painful experience.
We wish in this matter to be vary plain
with our working readers. We know how
much is occasionally suffered through impru-
dent strikes where, for want of discipline,
defeat is almost a certain consequence. And,
therefore, we say that the grand immediate
work for those who would lead amongst the
operatives of the country, is the work of orga-
nization. Union has now become possible, and
therefore a duty, for every class of operatives
whether in the fields, the factories, or the
workshops, and nothing but a culpable indif-
ference to its value can prevent any class
, of men from heartily pushing forward so
good a work. Agricultural labourers have
even become a manageable body ; their
ranks have been so thinned by removal of
large numbers to the manufacturing districts,
that the pressure of the unemployed does not
utterly disable those in employment from
taking action in their own interest. The same
May be said of the ordinary labourers in large
towns; to all these unionism has become a
Practicable duty, if they will take the steps
necessary to acquire its discipline, before they
rush wildly to grasp at its advantages.
The men employed on our railways are all
of them more or less skilled, and, therefore, for
this purpose possess more power over themselves
than utterly unskilled men; but as their em-
ployers are rich and powerful corporations, their
Organizations should be of the very best kind,
with a higher discipline and a wider-spread
Power than any other body of rnen ' stand in
need of. We say that this is necessary—if
the men decide to have anything to say as
regards their own condition whilst following
their employments ; but if it be better to leave
the matter in the hands of directors and
managers, then the less said about any
kind of united action the better. If a
capable and active assertion of their rights
be not within the power of anybody of work-
ing men, quietness, obedience, and content-
ment are indispensable duties. Whether such
a state of things is best for employers and
employed is another question. We think not.
We are convinced that it would be much more
advantageous for all parties if every branch of
employment was in union, and all differences
that might arise were subject to the arbitra-
tion of properly-appointed tribunals. Under
sueh nonditions all action would be orderly,
and every stop taken would have the advan-
tage of deliberate considerations. Nothing
can be worse than the oppressions sometimes
suffered by workers who have no power of
self-protection, and who occasionally rush
into contentions in which, as a rule, all

suffer, and nobody gains in any useful
way.

This porters' disaster should be a lesson to
all men situated as they are; and thorough
organization should, therefore, as a first step,
be made seoure. In fact, it should be the
principal, nay, the only work entered on till
it is complcte, and then concessions will come
without strikes, and improvements in the
men's condition will, of themselves, gradually
take place. The power to enforce a right is
the best warrant and surest guarantee for its
existence.

articles.title: OLD BOGIE.
articles.text:
OLD BOGIE.

SLESWICK-HOLSTEIN, though enjoying the
blessings of Prussian government, is not abso-
lutely safe nor entirely happy._ Its GovEßNon,
who is, no doubt, a most astute and
vigilant person, has had his fears awakened by
the incursions of Socialist agitators. He declares
that the country is oVerrun by them; that they
are spreading their ideas amongst the working
men, organizing strikes, and doing other evil
things, prejudicial to industry. Their object,
according to the -alarmed GOVERNOR, is to
overthrow everything the people love, respect,
and hold sacred—" The Fatherland, the
throne, the altar, morality and law, and to
substitute the public house for the home, to
dissolve the ties of property, and to reduce
labour, the nourisher and supporter of nations,
to the plaything of ambitious demagogues."
This, however, is only part of the charge as
given the other day in the Pall Mall Gazette,
but there is quite
_enough here to satisfy any
reasonable person that either these Socialist
emissaries are very simpre rascals, or that the
Governor Of SLESWIOIC is a person whose
excessive reverence for "property, 'order, and
religion," for the "throne and the altar," has
driven him foolishly frantic.
This is a very old kind of craze. The early
Christians were frequently charged with
making human sacrifices, and provincial
governors, all of whom were not so impartial
or so just as PLINY the younger, were ready
enough to promulgate such reports.. Crucifying
children used to be a periodical charge against
the .1-ews—their sins of the present day,' how-
over, are not of quite so dark a hue.
There are few things of which political or
religious knavery and folly are not capable.
In the warfare of opinions in the present day
men of all kinds, even provincial governors
ought, if possible, to keep themselves clear of
such miserable senseless slanders. If any
persons existed at the present time whose
object it was to do what the Socialists are
accused of by this GOVERNOR instead of
employing agitators to promulgate their
opinions, they weuld hide. themselves away
from the eyes of then, lest the' penalty of CAIN
should fall on them. A party ef men with
such objects never did exist and never can
exist,- but men onpable of making subh charges
are common enough. The worst specific
charge made, however, against these socialists
is the promoting of strikes, and that, we pre-
sume, whatever it may amount to in Sleswick
dees not in England moan an attack on
on the throne, o' r on the altar,
though probably there are persons who would
like very much to get up the cry that such was
the case.
The devil of the old monks was a most un-
pleasant creation. His saucer-eyes, his long
serpent-like tail, his claws, his ferked tongue,
and sulphurous smell, created a wholesome
horror in the public mind, and aided nurses
in keeping the children from being naughty.
The Internationalists and the Socialists of the
present day, whose moral deformity is as bad
as old BEELZEBUB'S physicalugliness, are used,
when occasion requires it, for much the same
purpose. When the children wanted what their
nurses did not wish to give them, or the
people troubled themselves about anything
displeasing to their spiritual advisers, the old
gentleman with the tail was shaken up and
made to roar. Now, when political and Social
rights are looked for by the people, the Inter-
nationalists and _Socialists are • turDed loose,
and thrones and altars are made to creak
mysteriously, and as a natural consequence
timid reformers draw in their heads and hold
their tongues lest everything should be brought
to a state of universal smash,

However, all mere tricks get. discovered in
time, and this last one is now pretty well
seen through, though,no doubt, when it is
thrown by as useless something else will be
found equally as efficacious in the hands of
knaves for the purpose of alarming the fat-
headed and foolish. ROBERT IYl.AcAutE's
maxim that, humbug is eternal, has not yet
been disproved.

articles.title: DIPLOMATIC ACKNOWLEDGMEMT OF' THE POPE'S SPIRITUAL POWER.
articles.text:
DIPLOMATIC ACKNOWLEDGMEMT OF'
THE POPE'S SPIRITUAL POWER.

TIIE ceaseless and determined antago-
nism of priestly influence and authority
to personal and public liberty, makes of
interest and importance to the bulk of all
nations every event and circumstance con-
nected. directly or indirectly with the Papacy
of Rome. In a small way, for example, the
British Government is one of those Govern-
ments which humour the heads of that con
spiracy against the rights of man, by sending
to the Vatican a kind of representative, apart'
from the more conspicuous envoy accredited to
the Court of Italy. Mr. MONK has raised a
question as to the rightness of this proceeding.
The POPE, he observes, is no longer a temporal
ruler; why, then, should we hold diplomatic
intercourse with him any more than with the
President of the Wesleyan Conference or the
Clerk of the Quakers' Annual Meeting? But,
if any such relations be kept up with the head
of that Church, they ought, at any
rate, to be strictly governed by the statute
under which, before his temporal power had
passed away, they were instituted and carried
on. Against this reasoning no argument can
prevail. Now, by that Act, it was provided
simply that a diplomatic agent of the British
Government should reside near the Sovereign
of the Roman States. But the POPE is no
longer such Sovereign; and consequently, the
statutory authority to send out an envoy to
him falls to the ground. That the States had
gone out of his hands could not be denied. It
was affirmed, however, that he still retained a
sovereign power over that portion of Rome
itself which is called the Leonine City, and
extends from the Bridge of Saint Angelo to
Saint Peter's Place. Nevertheless, as the
exactly informed are well aware, the King of
ITA.LY is the solo Sovereign of the country,
including the " Borgo " just described, no
loss than what used to be named "the States
of the Church' outside.

The inconvenience of having Sir AUGUSTUS
PAGET taking one view at the Royal Court
and Mr. CCM= SERVOISE another at the
Priestly Court, is obvious at a glance. But,
according to Sir COLMAN O'LoartLEN, the
latter gentleman is not accredited diplomati-
cally, but is a solitary individual who—when
the whole diplomatic body at Rome, hearing
the cannon of the Royal Army, packed up and
took to their heels—remained where he was,
not having any diplomatic mission or official
character whatever. How comes it, then, that
the estimates contain an item of £2OO as
allowance for his residence? Sir COLMAN made
no explanation of this official-looking fact;
instead of which, he relied upon another
statement, in the hope that it would up-
hold his argument. When- the Bill was
passing, the House of Lords inserted a
provision to the effect that the Roman Envoy
to England should bp a layman, in, CORSO-
quenoO of which the POPE declined sending
any representative at all, The learned
BARONET contends, indeed, that there is no
law against sending an envoy to the POPE;
but, supposing he were in ever so small a degree
a. temporal sovereign, both the principle and
the practice of diplomatio intercourse prescribe
that mutuality between the Po pE and the
QUEEN which characterises all diplomatic re-
lations whatsoever. The Foreign Office account
of the matter, as given by Lord ENFIELD,
hardly concurs with Sir C. 01LOGULEN'S notion
or pretence. Instead of saying with him that
Mr. JERVOISE is not accredited diplomatically,
the UNDER-SECRETA.Rr merely explains that he
corresponds with the Foreign Office directly and
not through Sir A. PA.GET (an arrangement
which may create inconvenience but not avoid
it), and gives us his word for it, that his ,
despatches do not express tiltramontane
sympathies (a thing for which we should look
in a man's public letters in a ratio inverse to

the strength of our conviction that he secretly
entertained them.)

It became the office of the ATTORNEY-
GENERAL a second time to explain his con-
ception of the state of the law on the question.
One thing he made certain enough, that he
"shifted his ease as a lawyer knows bow." In
his revised view of the matter, it made no
difference whether the POPE reigns in the
Leonie City or not, although that rag of tem-
poral authority had been essential for his
argument before. He now took his stand upon
the assertion, that there is no law bidding
intercourse between England and the mere
POPE, stripped.of alltemporality whatever. The
first statute of ELIZABETH is confined, he says,
in terms to spiritual authorityi Be it so, in
the total absence of temporal power, •what
other than spiritual can he retain P As to the
repeal, by an Act of the present reign, of the
penalties which the Fifth of ELIZA.BETH
imposed upon "extolling the pre-eminence of
the SEE of Rome,'' that is a point which affeets
the common liberty of speech rather than
diplomatic intercourse.

Sir Joror DUKE COLERTDOE, 'however, rests
the ease upon the Bill of Rights, with 11 and
12 Wrrairam M. By the former, as most
persons know, the Protestant succession to the
Crown is secured. By the latter, as ho oon-
tends, only religious and spiritual, and not
political and diplomatic intercourse between
the Crown and the wearer of the Tiara, is for
bidden. But then, admitting this distinction,.
it left the case under the governing
force of that mutuality of conditions
which evidently applies to all .diplomacy. The
act of 1.818, as he is forced to confess, ren-
dered lawful ' diplomatic intercourse on no
other than the usual and necessary terms, and
not with the POPE as mere head of his own
church, but as ho was, and so long as he
should continue to be, "Sovereign of the
Roman states." In support of his own view
of the question the ATTORNEY-GENERAI cited
several legal and constitutional authorities;
but it is observable that every, one of them
was antecedent to the fallof the POPE'S tem-
poral power; and, consequently, they lend no
force whatsoever to the ease as it now stands.

articles.title: Tin: SUPPLY OF MEAT.
articles.text:
Tin: SUPPLY OF MEAT.

Tim country gentlemen are naturally soli-
citous to keep away the cattle plague from
British pastures, and to prevent it from
spreading should it insinuate itself. They are
under a temptation, however, to make that
anxiety an excuse for subserviency to the
avarice of the home graziers. We hope,
therefore, that Mr. FORSTEIN complaisance to
members of Parliament of that class will not
be allowed to betray or compromise the con-
oilmen' interest in the adequate supply of food
at prices within reach of the community. He
specifies seven cargoes of diseased cattle. The
import from Russia is entirely prohibited, that
country being the fount and origin of the
evil. But, as theiVrcE-PnEsiDExx of Council
himself admits, he must,' like the PREMIER,
think thrice, if: not even oftener, before
making the interdict on Germany entire. The
effect, he knows, would be to diminish the
supply, especially to the London market, to an
extent so severe as nothing but absolute ne-
cessity could justify. Nevertheless, the infor-
mation he has from Hamburg left him no
choice but .- to exclude all animals from
Schleswig-Holstein, and to order the slaughter
on arrival in British ports of all sheep from
Germany. We candidly allow that he must
have hard work of it, between what he styles
"the natural fear of persons interested in the
trade," and the tendency of consumers to
charge his restrictions with increasing the
already high price of meat. But he must
remember the reputation he has already
acquired for being squeezable in the hands of
parsons and squires, and take care not to let
the " natural fears " of the latter drive him
t,OO far in the direction of their interested
wishes. Had not such "natural fears" been
steadily resisted, we should long arc now
have had a famine of bread, whieh, after all,
would be a much more serious.thing than a
scarcity' of meat.

A. any rate, Mr. FORSTER has not quite
relieved the "national fears " of Colonel
BARTTELOT and, his country clients. As the

Belgian Government has not excluded
German sheep, they may reach our shores
through Antwerp; and moreover, the foot and
mouth disease in cattle, introduced from
abroad, is represented to be spreading through
the length and breadth of England, and to have
shown itself in Ireland. Mr. FORSTER akain
pleads the difficulty of his position, the
difficulty, that is, of doing what is necessary,
but no more, As to the foot and. mouth
disease, the ',Government are doing what they
can in the Veterinary Department to arrest its
progress, but, believing it to be now at any
rate indigenous in this country, they have no
hope of success from further rostrictions on
foreign importation. :To do the right honour-
able gentleman justice, he has endeavoured to
mitigate the consequences of rigorous exclusion
in one direction by free admission in another.
Thus, cattle may be imported from France, if
slaughtered at the port of landing, the plague
having ceased in that country, and Brittany
affording prospects of considerablo.suPPly.
In the meantime, consideration is rife as to
the best means of encountering the pinch
which, under the best possible arrangements)
seems unavoidable. Those who rely upon
frugality counsel partial or total abstinence
from flesh meat. Those who fancy they see
ways out of the difficulty talk about
potted meats from Australia. Those who
think themselves masters of the whole
question point out certain alleviations of the
pressure. ',Perhaps it is not quite impossible
to checkmate the greedy dealers who double the
increase of price which scarcity occasions before
they will allow us to have a mouthful, by
being content with one ounce where we used
to induldge ourselves with three. Potted
meat from Melbourne would take some time
to make and send; and, moreover, it smacks
of the remedy proposed by the French
Duchess who, when bread was dear,
suggested pastry. But, as Mr. GAMGEE asks,
where is effective labour to come from, if
working MOII be not paid at rates which will
enable them to buy necessary food? That is
the point; and country gentlemen, laying aside
their "natural fears,' had better unite with all
the rest in honestly deliberating on the best
means of dividing to every man according to
kis " natural " needs and his just claims.

At any rate, a man so.high in his profession
as Mr. GAMGEE claims a hearing from all
parties. Ile declares that we have not lost a
tithe by the Russian murrain that we have by
lung and foot and mouth disease. These alone
have wasted not less than three hundred mil-
lions sterling worth of meat since 1842, and,
instead of efforts being directed towards their
extinction, wo meet and talk about stopping
the slaughter of calves, which mainly come to
us from abroad, and lambs, which people will
eat in spite of remonstrance. Under existing
regulations, neither the lung nor the foot and
mouth complaint can he held in check whilst a
single animal, except Spanish cattle, is per-
mitted to pass through a slaughter-house
alive, at the ports where foreign beasts ore
landed. The proper method of dealing with
the question involves, first, rational disease
prevention measures on the farms where the
foreign plagues appear; second, perfect free-
dom for healthy British or Irish cattle ; third,
absolute o.nd permanent exclusion of foreign
live animal's front contact with our own in
markets or elsewhere. .Irish cattle spread dis-
ease, but only disease we send to Ireland, or
communicate to Irish cattle on their transit.
This sounds like the science of common sense.

THE BANK HOLIDAYS ACT IN LONDON.
Taking advantage of Sir John Lubbock's Bank
Holidays Act the most tempting inducements were
on Monday offered by the railway and steamboat
companies to excursionists, but the influence of
the weather did not tend to heighten the anticipa-
tion of those catering for "a day at the sea-side"
or "a cheap trip" to other places of favourite
resort. Notwithstanding an advance of one shil-
ling on the popular "three shillings there and
back" there were two thousand three hundred
persons conveyed (in four trains) to Brighton via
the London, Brighton, and South Coast Line, and
two other excursion trains sufficed for the traffic
by the same company for Hastings in the one
direction, and Portsmouth, for Southsea and the
Isle of Wight, in the other. Thoso booking for
gortimouth seem to have been very unfortunate

with respect to the weather. By the South East-
ern line two excursion trains were despatched to
Hastings; one to Ramsgate and Margate; one to
Dover; and hur to Gravesend. These were in
addition to the ordinary traffic; and an Odd
Fellows and Foresters' fête in Knob ° Park, Seven-
oaks, caused some attraction in that direction.
Only one train was required to meet the demand
at Ludgate-hill for excursionists to Canterbury
and Dover, and one for Ramsgate and Broadstairs ;
and the "special cheap train" to Portsmouth,
Southsea, and. Southampton, for the Isle of Wight,
leaving the South Western Terminus, Waterloo,
at ten minutes past seven, was crowded. Nor did
the inclement weather deter the many proceeding
to Waterloo from booking to Windsor, Hampton
Court, Richmond, Sze. Although about 17,000
left London-bridge for the .Crystal Palace, the
High-level from Ludgate-hill to Sydenham was
not much patronised. The London and North-
Western, Great Western, Great Northern, &c.,
each submitted long journeys at cheap
tariffs. In spite of the weather the steamboats
plying "below bridge" experienced a goodly
amount of patronage. The Alexandra saloon
boat left London-bridge at 9.45 with a heavy
freight for Gravesend, and the Palmerston left
the same pier at 10.30 with an equal number on
board for, Sheerness, &c. Fcom.the same starting
point the saloon and other steamers of the Wool-
wich Steam Packet Company were despatched for
Gravesend, Southend, Sheerness, &c., the first
boat leaving at nine o'clock, and tho seventh and
last at three o'clock. The traffic up the river was
very indifferent.

articles.title: PENNY-A-LINING AND WORKING MEN'S
articles.text:
PENNY-A-LINING AND WORKING MEN'S

DEMONSTRATIONS.

This is a profession of which there are many
varieties, but that which is most active in times
of political or social excitement is composed of
those least scrupulous as to persons and circum.
stances.

The Stamford Mercury and the .Peterborough
Times are both served by a person of this kind,
and his report of the Peterborough Agricultural
Labourers' Demonstration, held July 27, and
printed in both those papers, is as good a specimen
of the kind of article these gentlemen deal in as
could be well furnished. First, the sentences are
slightly transposed and the facts altered so as to
destroy identity, though the thing .is so clumsily
done as to be plain to the merest tyro in composi-
tion. Then the falsehood which is meant to be
circulated is put in as if it had proceeded from
two pens instead of ono—that is, the writer
invents his lie for the one paper, and corroborates
in the other. He states that a meeting of aboN
12,000 only numbered about ],óOo; and against
an assemblage, orderly in the highest degree, he
brings a charge of drunkenness and disorder, so
Utterly false that it is impossible it could have
been concocted by any sober man who felt himself
open to detection and exposure.
Penny-a-lining, like everything else, may be
made respectable by the spirit in which it is
carried on; but so many take to it who have
broken down in other pursuits, either through
stupidity or want of necessary good conduct, that it
is no wonder the news paragraphs of the above
mentioned papers are occasionally disgraced by
libels against the working people, which nobody
but broken down pettifoggers or disgraced bum-
bailiffs could possibly think of promulgating.

INTEGRITY LIFE ASSURANCE AND
SICK. BENEFIT SOCIETY.

The fourteenth annual general meeting of the
members of this society was held on Monday at
Arundel Hall, Arundel-street, Strand, Mr. Nash
occupying the chair.
The report and balance-sheet were read by Mr.
Travers, the secretary, and accepted by the meet-
ing. The committee, in reviewing the operations
of the "Integrity" for the year 1871, stated that
the total number of proposals received during the
year amounted to 18,174, producing in weekly
premiums upwards of £137. The cash account
showed a premium income of £20,015 Is. id.;
and the claims paid during the year made a total
of £13,016 12s. 7d.—an amount somewhat more
than anticipated by the committee, but sufficiently
accounted for by the general high rate of mor-
tality. The members now numbered upwards of
60,000. It had been considered conducive to the
prosperity of the life branch to restrict and isolate
the sick business, with a view of conducting it as
a separate society, and several meetings had been
held during the year for the purpose of discussing
' and framing a new code of rules, which had now
been agreed upon.

The report and balance-sheet having been
unanimously accepted, the meeting was subse-
quently addressed by Mr. Searle, Mr, O'Leary.
Idr, Maloney, Mr. O'StilliTan, Mr. OtelrenS, and

others, and votes of thanks were passed to the
committee of management and to the secretary.

UNIVERSAL BENEFICENT SOCIETY.

The Lord Mayor presided on Tuesday at a
meeting held at the Mansion-house, with a view
of extending the operatiofts of this society, which
was founded to assist in various ways those in
necessity, of good character, without distinction
of cuss, nationality or sect. The Lady Mayoress,
the Marquis and Marchioness of Townshend, and
others were present. The Chairman, in opening
the proceedings, briefly set forth the objects of the
meeting, which he said were not so much to advo-
cate the claims of the society on the public gene-
rally as to endeavour to organize a something by
passing resolutions which should draw the atten-
tion of the different municipalities throughout the
country to what they proposed to do. He be-
lieved that if the intentions of the society were
disseminated throughout the length and breadth
of the land a very great benefit would arise to it.
The Marquis Townshend moved, "That in the
opinion of this meeting it is desirable that the
operations of the Universal Beneficent Society be
extended by branches throughout the United
Kingdom." This was seconded by Captain Nor-
cliff o Gilpin and carried. A resolution was also
proposed and adopted to the effect that the Lord
Mayor be requested to invite the co-operation of
the municipal authorities throughout the kingdom
in furtherance of the foregoing resolution. A vote
of thanks to the chairman terminated the proceed-
ings.

articles.title: IMPROVED DWELLINGS FOR THE WORKING CLASSES.
articles.text:
IMPROVED DWELLINGS FOR THE
WORKING CLASSES.

On Wednesday, at the Mansion-house,
Alderman Sir Sydney Waterlow, the chair-
man, presided at the eighteenth half-yearly
meeting of the Improved Industrial Dwellings
Company, and was supported by, among
others, Mr. Alderman Finnis, Sir 'William
Bodkin, Sir Francis Hicks, the Rev. Thomas
Wodehouse, Mr. A. B. Daniell, Mr. John
Griffith, and Mr. James Moore (the secretary).
The report stated that the subscribed capital
now amounted to £206,150, and the nu-
allotted shares represented £43,850. The
loans from the Public Works Commissioners
were to the amount of £84,000 in all, of
which £69,000 had been received. The rents
during the half-year had brought in £9,483,
and the total expenditure was £5,294, leaving
a profit of upwards of £4,000. The directors
recommended the payment of the usual divi-
dend of five per cent., and that from the

articles.title: BISHOP ON THE LABOUR QUESTION.
articles.text:
A BISHOP ON THE LABOUR
QUESTION.

The Bishop of Gloucester and Bristol,
Dr. Ellicott, in responding to the toast of
"The Bishop and Clergy of the Diocese," at
the annual dinner of the Gloucestershire Agri.
cultural Society, which closed its exhibition
at Gloucester on Friday, referred at seine
length to the labour question. His Lordship
said we now lived in very trying times--
times in which mischievous and evil efforts
were being made to set class against class, and
especially to set faithful English labourers
against their equally faithful English em-
ployers. Although to his regret he had heard.
of certain meetings being held, and of some
agitation going on in certain quarters, he
claimed that Gloucestershire had up to the
present time enjoyed great immunity, princi-
pally because the labourers knew that what-
ever equitable demands were made by the
labourers, if made respectfully, the employers
were thoroughly ready to respond to the ap.•
plication. Several months ago many of the
Gloucestershire farmers nobly came forward
and raised the wages of the different persons
they employed on their estates. And why ?
Because they were underpaid? By.no means,
but because they saw this anxious rise in prices
everywhere, and because they reasoned as
good, plain, honest Englishmen that if money
would purchase less than it did in former
times, of course more money must be given for
the honest efforts of the muscles and sinews
of the labourer ; and so, recognizing that money
was generally sinking in value, they at once
came forward and said, "If you have to pay
more for your meat "—andit was not often, he
was afraid, the labourers could get meat—" it
is right I should pay more for these brawny
arms and. hands that till my fields. "
On behalf of the labourers he also wished to
say a few words. There had been a few
improper agitations among them. He could
not condemn in too strong terms, or denounce
too severely, those who came from afar—men
who never owned an acre, men who never did
a day's work—into their welds and peaceful
villages, seeking out the disaffected everywhere
—making iniquitous combinations, and setting
English employers against English labourers.
He denounced theta as strongly as any man
could denounce any ma-English proceeding,
and it was not for him, a man of peace, to
say anything stronger than that he hoped all
his friends would keep the race, and remember
their bishop advised them that if the village
horsepond stood invitingly near, not by any
means to put these men into it. He had given
this advice, and. he hoped it would be
followed; perhaps it would be hard, but they
must resist the temptation. It might be
that the labourers had received too little
money, but they had had their wages made up
by other things, and. there were two sides even
to that question. He heard the other day a
most distinguished employer of labour say at a
public meeting in London that he had to pay
each of his hands 2s. td. a day, and something
more at the end of the week; and he said
publicly that the amount of drunkenness had
increased frightfully, and that the women
came to complain that the men put this money
into their pockets and carried it every evening
to the alehouse. So there were two sides to
the question, and they must hesitate to
denounce very severely the truck system,
where, in addition to wages, were given the
value of a cottage, or those other friendly
gifts which were and could be given, and
which went far to induce the family to keep
the home together. He had no sympathy
with that tendency to set class against class
which persons in good position had thought
it necessary to pursue in other counties *by
deporting labourers from their county to other
parts of the country. Lot them cultivate
kindly relations among the men, and he waa
sure the clergy would. do their best in the
matter. The English labourer and farmer
must, if it was only for their own interest,
remain united, but they were byund with a
better bond than that—as common sons of an
ancient and honourable country; and ill in-
deed would be the day when the interests of
the English labourer were supposed not to be
identical with those of the British farmer.

Mr. W. P. Price, M.P., in responding to
the toast of the "Members for the Boroughs,"
also referred to the labour question, saying
that probably there was no man in that large
assembly who was brought more into contact
with it than himself. He was afraid there
was some little misunderstanding on the sub-
ject. The question of wages was not really a
question ot so many shillings a week, for
there could be no possible doubt of this fact,
that a sovereign was not now worth what a
sovereign was. He was perfectly persuaded
that the labourer must be remunerated on a
higher scale measured by shillings, than here-
tofore, and by so doing they would net be
paying higher wages to the labourer, nor be
giving him a larger power of control over the
necessaries of life. Mr. Price also argued in
favour of better dwellings for the agricultural
labourers, and expressed his belief that the
farmers would do well in giving them a bit of
laud in addition. If all this was done he be-
lieved we should have as contented a popula,
tion as ever we had before.

AUG. 10, 1872.
