THE COAL MINERS.
To the Editor of the BEE-HIVE.
Srn,—As a constant subscriber of your
paper, and also as a coal miner, I hope you
will allow me the privilege of placing my
humble opinions before your readers in regard
to the Mines Regulation Bill. No doubt yen
will see that they are different to those of Mr.
McDonald and others' for, while they say that
a better friend than Lord Elcho we • miners
could not have I judge him quite
differently, as I think a greater opponent of
nearly all that the miners require could
scarcely be found • for instance, of all the
points that Mr. found;
says that Lord
Elcho has supported, there is two whioh I will
mention—the first is the clause that gives
three months' imprisonment to the owner of a
mine for a violation of certain provisions. It
is remarkable that during the last three
sessions Lord Elcho has opposed this very
thing, and not supported it as Mr. McDonald
says. For a ease I will give you Lord Elcho's
remarks on this very clause when it was
introduced this session, namely, he said it
would he manifestly unfair that the owner of
a mine who might be in Rome should be held
responsible for an accident in his mine in
England. The other point that Mr. McDonald
says he has supported is one of the most im-
portant in the Bill: it is the ventilation clause.
You are quite aware that almost everybody
admits that a more efficient system of ventila-
tion is necessary, and Mr. Bruce, the Home
Secretary, gives us miners all that is desired
for ventilation purposes in his Bill; but my Lord
Etch° and the mine agents have assisted the
coal owners by saying that the present system
of ventilation in the mines of this country is
sufficient and needs no alteration. I will again
trouble you with Lord Elcho remarks in
reference to the ventilation clause, namely,
-whilst listening to this discussion he could not
help thinking it would be desirable to have a
barometer in this house, in order that hon.
members might know what kind of atmosphere
pervaded it; if the barometer had shown that
explosive gases were afloat, hon, gentlemen
would have known that there were a great
number of blowers on the Treasury Bench
to-day, and, that at all events one of the
volcanoes on that bench was not extinct. His
right hon. friend the Secretary of State
, said the interest of the miners had
been betrayed. He distinctly asked the
right hon. gentleman to state who it was that
had betrayed the cause of the miner. The
impression made upon practical men by the
right hon. gentleman's new-born zeal was this,
that he was endeavouring to putnpon the mine
owners duties, which, owing to the laws of
nature it was impossible for them to fulfil.
This question was discussed years ago before
this unholy alliance had been formed; it was
discussed at meetings of miners and coal-
owners, and they agreed on a form of words
which they thought unexceptionable, namely,
except under circumstances that could not
reasonably have been anticipated. He hoped
the right hon. gentleman would not fly at his
throat again—(oh, oh,)—morally he meant—
for referring to the meetings which were held
this year with respect to the Bill; the words
he mentioned were proposed, and who was it
that objected to them? Mr. Dickinson, one of
the inspeotors, and his reason was that the
words could not be constructed to moan more
than the words under ordinary circumstances.
After Lord Elcho had opposed this clause
for better ventilation (which Mr. McDonald
says he supported), Mr. Cranford answered
Lord Eloho's opposition to the clause in the
following words, namely :—he contended that
the clause should be retained in the Bill as it
stood in the interest of the miners, whose lives
were in danger. He must object to the words
ordinary circumstances, or any other
words being inserted for any qualification of
the clause would be a means of escape from
that liability which they were anxious to
impose on the masters, the arguments against
the clause, were in fact, arguments against
the legislation, which the House of Commons
had expressed its determination to adopt. He
earnestly hoped that her Majesty's Govern-
ment would stick to thoir own clause also. I
will give you some remarks in support of the
same clause by another friend of the miners,
Dr. Lyon Playfair, who said he dissented
entirely from the words "under ordinary cir-
cumstances." Now, what would be thought of
a proposal to make the captains of ships
only responsible for navigating their vessels
under ordinary circumstances. (Hear, hear.)
If the barometer fell, and if a hurricane
came on, was the captain's responsibility to
cease? Why, then, should the responsibility
of the mine-owner be at an en 4 when the
barometer fell, and a moment of danger was
at-hand. '7l per cent. of the explosions were
due to barometical depressions and therro.o-
metrical risings. It was highly important,
therefore, that the owners should be made

responsible for meeting the danger when the
barometer fell. He himself had a considerable
interest in mines, and he felt convinced that
both the owners and the miners would be
benefited if this responsibility was imposed on
the coalowners.

In a letter last week sent by Mr. McDonald,
and which appeared in your paper, he states
that they, the agents, only compromised the
words "under ordinary circumstances," to be
inserted into Mr. Bruce's Bill (which would
take away all the good out of the clause
by their insertion) was only agreed to on the
16th of June. I say, on the contrary, that
they were agreed to in the middle of March.
For proof of this Mr. Pickard states, fresh from
the conference in London at a delegate meet-
ing in Wigan in the Public Hall, and re-
ported in both of the Wigan papers and
a great many of the daily papers,
that they, the agents, had submitted to
the inSertion of the words "under ordinary
circumstances." So much for Mr. McDonald's
statements; and also Mr. Pickard states
that they, the agents, had submitted to
the educational clause for the boys being
withdrawn from the Bill, and also the clauses
with respect to certified efficient managers of
mines which could not be mended, and for the
insertion of something in their stead which
none in the House could understand, or make
anything of, only the coalowners; besides a
great many other alterations in other clauses
right through the Bill, which I could enume-
rate if space would allow. I can defy Mr.
McDonald and all the agents put together,
Lord Elcho included, that greater opponents
to the real interests of the miners could not
be found than they themselves, as they had
been pledged for the very things which
they have opposed; and . I say further that
there has not been a single petition pre-
sented to Parliament that has not asked for
the very things that• they have opposed,
further, I defy Chem to produce from any of
the papers, of all the speeches that
Lord Elcho has made on the Bill,
forty lines in support of any of its clauses,
though he has been styled by them as the best
friend that we could have had. Now, sir, with
your permission I will mention who has been a
better friend to us than my Lord Etch°, viz.,
Mr. A. J. Mundella, who has stood up for
the miners nobly; yet Mr. McDonald a few
weeks ago, speaking at the miners' meeting at
Durham, where there was 50,000 or 60,000
miners present, and was reported in the
Durham Chronicle, he incited the miners to
cry out aloud shame on Mr. Mundella, which
they in their ignorance did, for he is like a
dumb dog towards the miners and the work-
ing classes generally; and when his re-elec-
tion comes round, he, Mr. McDonald, threatens
to meet him in Paradise-square, Sheffield. If
he carries out his.threat, I believe the wotk-
ing people of Sheffield would do honour to
themselves by kicking him out of the town,
for they, like the working classes throughout
the country, know that they have in Mr.
Mundella a real representative, and one that
does credit to them. In conclusion, the Bill is
almost got through both Houses, but not in
the good condition it was, as introduced by the
Government. The Bill has been greatly de-
layed and damaged by the agents and Lord
Elcho who have been playing hand and glove
with the coalowners instead of supporting the
Government and others in trying to improve
it where it was possible. Hoping you will
insert this and do justice to both sides of the
queition,4 am, yours, &e.,
AN OLDIIAM MINEU.

THE CURRENCY.
To the Editor of the BEE-HIVE.
SlR,—Paper issues by Governments must
surely be as feasible a matter as paper issues
by individuals humble subjects only of
such Governments. Moreover, the former
assuredly must command far more of public)
confidence than the latter. Therefore, apro-
position involving the exchange of a private
for a public paper circulation, can hardly be a
matter deeply to be deprecated. Were it
otherwise, however, it, at least, cannot be
said that I stand done in making such a pro-
position. Indeed, in this matter I travel in very
excellent company!
One of the prime objections raised against
the 'paper-forni of money, is its liability to over-
issues, and consequently to early depreciation.
Under the propositions of my former letters,
however, in oonnection with the optional
deposit of mites of the form and purpose
proposed, over - issues, and consequently
depreciation, _would be impossible, since any
surplus issue would always very sOO/1
find its way into the public banks, asso-
ciated (as suggested by me Many years
since, as well as in my recent letters) with .the
principal post offices.
Besides, the right of resumption advocated
by me heretofore, in connection with such
notes, when so deposited with direct liability
to such resumption, would, on the other hand,
obviate anything like a dearth of money in
circulation, at any time, so that a paper circu-
lation, under such a system, wouli evidently
promise to be self-regulative. Further, in
confirmation of this view, it may be stated
that the claimants of all notes deposited
(though not permanently deposited) would be
likely, collectively, in every county to con-
stitute (so to call them) public) loan societies
on mdre equitable principles than many which
now privately bear that name.
Meanwhile taxation in the form proposed,
lighter in its aggregate amount, would be
lighter also in the form of its incidence—the
amount of taxation borne by any man under
such circumstances being, moreover, a sure
indication of the extent of his property; and,
therefore, no grievance to him. Again, the
proposed mode would induce to a great extent
cash, rather than credit, transactions, as no
man having money could, under such circum-
stances, keep it back from his creditors
without, as it were, burning his own,
fingers. Indeed, money under such ti
system would often probably, where tradesmen
appeared worthy of such confidence, be paid
beforehand—goods being called for at con-
venience. Finally, such a system knowing
neither surplus nor deficit in its results, one
hundred millions at a decline of a farthing per
day; fifty millions at a decline of a halfpenny
per day; or twenty-five millions at a decline
of a penny per day—sections of such rate of
decline being, in certain oases, associated with
special sections of each business day—would
each—with due renewals—raise thirty millions
per annum. A similar sum also at the latter
rate could be raised by twelve and a half
millions of ten shilling notes or by six and a
quarter millions of five shilling notes. Any
other amounts of issue at any other rate of
decline, and with notes of any other value,
realising always with precision strictly pro-
portional results, and thus opening a ready
way to a perfect consummation of Free Trade.
Taxation being thus removed from com-
modities and placed in the cheapest poulible
form on money itself; on money, the grandest
of all luxuries; on money in circulation, and
on money in deposit.—l am Sir, yours, &e.,
W. A. RUSSELL.
Collegiate School, Greenwich.

he must bear in mind that it was himself that
started it, and he must likewise conceive
that such a tissue of falsehoods eould. not be
Palmed on the public without injury to our-
selves, and an intelligent body of joiners are not
the men to let him have it all his own way. As
regards the word dishonourablej still maintain
the word is rightly placed, as a good Many of
his own trade are dlssati4lied with his terms,
and the public opinion is if the masons had
stood fast, the whole affair, would' have been
settled long ago. Mr. Broadhurst takes so
much credit to himself on the great success
and the terms he has made., and was about
addressing the joiners at the' Brown Bear •,
but discretion proved the better part of
valour for once with him. He need see no fear
that his name will be forgotten in the build-
ing trade for some years as the leader that
sold the short time movement. Mr. Broad-
hurst terms mine talk, talk. I consider
his very small talk when lie is aware
that all joiners, honourable enough -to
join in this movement, have refused to work
overtime for months past. Of course our
trade is not infallible any more than his own
thirty thousand. How Mr. Broadhurst can
say they did not try to maintain the short
hours in February, I cannot imagine; but his
memory must have failed him in that as well
many other things. Ile says Mr. Mitchley
and his committee are Buttering with Bir-
mingham on the brain. I beg to tell him I
have no committee,' or am I a committee man
on this movement, but I have a recollection of

came out for nine hours in 1854—that is just
five years before the nine ' hours was ever
tried at—but he gets his date frern my former
letter, in which a misprint occurred. It should
have read 1859 instead of • 1854 when the

but he seems to be very ignorant about the
former mOvements. I can supply. him with a
balance sheet of the 70. Movement of the
carpenters to refresh his memory, knowing
that his• trade never possessed one.—Yours, &e.,
J OUN MITCIILEY, 'Joiner.

THE COAL TRADE.
To the Edior of the BKE-Ffivn.

Ihn,—The Times of Aug. G reports a great ex-
citement in the coal trade. At the meeting o
the Northern Union of Mechanics' Institutions,
at Blythe, the president, Mr. H. Taylor, one
of the principal Northumberland coal-owners,
stated that one of the reasons of the great cry
for coal was the enormous increase of the iron
trade, for which it might be supposed four
millions was requisite. Another reason, he
said,. was the additional supplies of coal
wanted on account of the prosperity of the
manufacturers of the Tyne, and also the
inereaseddemands of the steam shipping trade.
He thought that the root of the evil lay in
the "short output of coal in the United King-
dom," which was ten millions of tons less this
year than last. This he attributed, to the
reduetion.of, the hours of labour, which had
been over 20 per cent.; and added that a rise
in the price of coal must be expeoted, "unless
they could work the quantity to meet all the
donne& of the country." The export of coals
htd increased this year half a million of tons,
and foreigners, finding that coal was clearer;
were securing their supplies for fear of a fur-
ther rise in the price of coal. Besides this
many of the collieries were short of hands'
And tho pitmen of the North had shortened'
their hours of work.

F. DICKINSON,
Kingweston, Somerton, Taunton.
THE AGRICULTURAL LABOURER.
To the Editor of the BER:Htvg.
•
Salt —Having read a letter, signed" C. H.
Novae," in your last, permit me to say that
SO far as Herefordshire is concerned, the
highest wages are 12s. a week, not 15s. to 18s,
as stated in the return he takes for his autho;
rity. Now, as I have no desire to "falsify
facts to serve my argument," permit me to
give the utterances of a few labourers who
were addressed at Pencombe a few evenings
since, by myself and my friend, Mr. Strange.
The meeting wail held in the school-room of
the place, under the chairmanship of the Rev.
G. Arkwright, brother to the employer of the
labourers, and brother to R. A.rkwrlght, who
represents Leominster in Parliament. By

personal enquiries I can vouch for the truth
of the following statements :
(It must not be forgotten that the employer
here referred to is one of the most deservedly
popular men in the county of Hereford.)
John Knight, labourer, had a wife and five
children, four at home. Wages lie, a week.
Had to buy half-a-bushel and half-a,peck of flour
each. week. Then there was rent and taxes. The
low wages makes me have to pick up) what wood I
can. . Some days last winter we had to go without
fire. It seems as if it is impossible for me to pass
by it. If I did I should be destroying the home
comforts of my own family. This is the truth,
and so I'll say it here.
James Phillips, labourer, todertham, worked
on the estate of Mr. J. IL Arkweight. Had a
wife and seven children—six at home, and when
he had to send the other from home it almost
tripped them. Wages lie, a week and no cider.
Hoped they should be soon able to get more.
Bread and cheese four days a week- no cheese
two days. Sometimes he had to gather docks
and nettles and boil them to eat. This is the
truth. •

• Henry Lawrence, labourer, Boienham, worked
for Mr. .T. it. Arkwright. Had Ils, a week and
no cider. Had a wife and four children ; wife
an invalid and one child a cripple. Bought half
a bushel of flour a week. Was in debt now and
likely to be, but hoped with better wages he
should be able to alter it a bit. He gravely added,
"I'm over head and ears in debt, and starvation
would have been the lot of my family had not
our friends helped us."
Henry Betthell, labourer, Bodenham' worked
for Mr. J. 11. Arkwright. Was not so bad off as
-those who had his., but it was as much as he
could do to keep out of debt; he was working at
tabk day-work in quarries. "Till we have done
the work we don't know what pay we shall get
for it. We. are -generally told we shall be paid
what it is worth, but it is generally about the
same as farm labourers' wages. It is an uncom-
mon bad system and wants altering." No cider
was allowed, and he preferred the money to the
drink, as he could buy it if he wanted it. He had
drunk eider as had made him feel bad.
George Hope, an aged labourer, got Is. 4d. a-day
when able. He had to live 'on ss, a week and
sometimes loss, because ho could not always get, to
work.
Charles Buck, waggoner, employed on Mr. J. H.
Arkwright's 'estate, had 12s. a week—no cider.
He worked from 5 a.m. till 7.30 p.m. in the
winter, and somatimes he was amongst the horses
till as late as nine o'clock in the summer. A
waggoner had to be out in all weathers, and his
clothes had often to dry on his back. He thought
waggoners ought to have more wages. Sometimes
in the winter he had to take food whilst feeding
his pig. This was the truth, and he did not wish
to deny it,. _

George Price, labourer, had five children, two of
which Ito could not afford to send to school ; ho
should be glad to do so.

These are "scenes which do exist," and
during eighteen months agitation many such
statements are made in public meeting by the
labourers.

We have been the means of getting wages
up to 12s. a week in some cases, but until we
have made arrangements for a conference of
the branches we have formed, I must say
there is very little chance of Mr. Nevile's
assertion being true. I only wish that it was
so now; we would "lay down our oars" with
thankfulness.

I really do think that Mr. Nevile ought to
have remembered that the organ he quotes
from is a farmer's paper, not an advocate of
the labourer.

C. MASTERS BLACKWELL.
West of England Farm Labourers' Im-
provement Society, Leominster.

P.S.---The agitation for the amelioration of
the condition of the labourer is still going on.
Any donation from your readers will be gladly
received by Mr. Strange, Adforton, or myself.

ANNUAL EXCURSION OF WORICHEN'S

THE SOUTH WALES MINERS.
To the Editor of the BEE-HIVE.
Sin,—The dispute in the house coal trade
has culminated into a strike. By the time
this appears in print the men will have been
out a fortnight. Our request is 4d. per ton,
or less than id. per hundredweight. Our
employers say ivo shall not have it; hence the
strike. Our present demand and the advance
we obtained for the last eighteen months do
not amount to more than 10d. per ton, or less
than 4d. per hundredweight. These are the

facts. We are not asking over one-fourth of
what is our due, therefore let the public judge
between us. From ten to twelve colliery pro-
prietors in this district have given the advance
to their men, and in Monmouthshire, the ad-
joining county, a large number of coal owners
have given the advance to their men, there-
fore we are compelled to resist, or be the
means of reducing all those who have obtained
the advance. We hereby make an appeal to
the colliers, working men, and the public at
large for support by subscriptions, addressed
to Mr. George Coles, Perth, Rhondda Valley,
Pontypridd, South Wales, but made payable
at the Perth Post Office to Mr. Richard Lane,
New York Inn, Perth, 4hondda Valley,
Pontypridd, South Wales.
Caution to the Public.—No moneys to be
paid to any person on behalf of the men on
strike unless authorised by the committee,
with the seal of the Rhondda District attached.
We hope to have the sympathy of the colliers
in particular, and all working men in general,
and the public at large. We have no funds
in hand.—We are, yours truly,
TnE COMMITTEE.

THE HIGH PRICE OF COAL AND FOOD.
To the Editor of the "BEE-HIVE."

Sin,—A. very able article appeared in your
last week's issue on the puke of coal, from the
pen of A. McDonald, the writer's object
being to show the public that the advanced
price of coal does not go to any great extent
into the pockets of the labourers, in which I
agree with him as far as he goes. I would,
however, venture to say that he ought to have
gone a little further; for instance, there are
two or three reasons more besides the six he
placed before your readers why coals are dear.
First. There is the increrse in the quantity
exported.
Second. There is the increased quantity
wasted in the British navy, which is unneces-
sary during the times of profound peace.
Thirdly and lastly, though not by any
means the least, there is the almost famine
prices of the raw material—that feeds (or
ought to feed)—our labouring classes whilst
they are toiling to get the supply of coal up
to the demand.

I will dwell principally on the third point,
inasmuch as it involves a problem which once
solved the ground is clear for the solution of
that difficult question, viz., the quarrel be-
tween labour and capital.
Capital and labour are bound together by
the mutual ties of self-preservation, natural
laws, and laws divine; and were it not that
the fiscal laws of the land are at war with the
natural laws of supply and demand, capital
and labour would find their own level in
mutual good understanding in the nature of
of things as water runs down hill. It has
been pointed out repeatedly in these columns,
and notably in the BEE-HIVE of March 30th,
page 3, how the fiscal laws of the land tend to
set capital and labour by the ears. But it
cannot be too often repeated until we have
these laws rooted out from the face of the
"Statute Book."
Coal is the article that has made this
country what she is; not only coal, but cheap
coal. Once get coal permanently, or oven flue-
tuatingly, above a certain average value in
England, and you strike a blow at the great-
ness of this country, as a nation, as disastrous
as that of a foreign enemy landing with a
million hostile soldiers, or a civil war, which
lay waste London, Liverpool, Manchester,
Glasgow, and all our great seats of industry.
What, then, is it that prevents the possi-
bility of the supply of coal increasing with the
increased demand? Not the advance in the
price of labour for getting, as Mr. Macdonald
has shown, except to a very small extent; but
there are collateral influences connected with
strikes and lock-outs which go a great way
towards it; they, for instance, stop the opera-
tion of getting to an enormous extent, and
then come on us short supplies, seeing that
consumption and export are increasing in place
of stopping (especially in the export depart-
ment) all the while. This causes the bulk of
the advance price to gravitate round the
homes of the rich.

Now What we wish to point out is the influ-
ence that high prices of provisions (or the
necessaries and comforts of life) have upon the
price of coal, as, iii fact, upon high prices
generally. As an illustration we will take the
ease of the present agitation now going on in
the coal and iron districts, and in all the in-
dustrial districts. There is a mutual recri-
mination going on between the producer of coal
and the producer of the raw material on which
ths life and health of the producer of coal de-
pends, viz., the butcher.
Labourers in coal mines meet in solemn eon.
olave and denounce the butchers for charginc,
extortionate prices for meat. The latter, in self-
defence, meet in like manner and denounce
the former for charging extortionate prices for
their fuel; this is the case of every industry
and every class in the country, which is
throwing all our industrial and social life into
a state of chaos.

In order to economise space and time we
would refer our readers (for a further explana-
tion) to another column in this paper, where the
writer further develcpes the question under
the head of "High Price of Butchers' Meat,

Atro: 10, 1872.

its Causes and Remedy." Suffice it to saY
that before leaving the subject we would re-
commend Mr. Macdonald and his coadjutor 3
to get up a conference for the express purpose
of discussing the question as to how far it is
desirable to continue the present fiscal system,
or whetherit is not for the good of all classes
torepeal the duties on tea, coffee, tobacco, malt,
sugar, wine, spirits, and every other article of
commerce, and in place thereof to levy the
taxes in the way pointed out in our columns
of this day's issue.

Tnos. BaIGOL
The Homestead, Richmond, Surrey.
August 7th, 1872.

THE ARTIZANS DWELLINGS COM-

PANY.

With "a new": phrase, the rrelevaney of
which was instantly avouched by the ap-
plause of his hearers the Earl of Shaftesbury
defined the project lie was called on to ini-
tiate, on Saturday, at Wandsworth. "We
have founded this day," said his lordship, "a
Workmen's City; and we have: founded it
upon the very best principles." These, as the
noble earl went on to explain, were the
principles of self-help and independence—the
last being entirely compatible with the free
acceptance of sympathy and aid, whioli every
man, great or small, stands in need of from his
fellows. Having laboured earnestly and strenu-
ously for more than thirty years in advocating
domiciliary improvement, as the first and best
means of improving the people, Lord Shaftes-
bury, above all men, was in his right place
when helping prominently at the foundation
of dwelling-houses, to be erected by the
Artizans', Labourers', and General Dwellings
Company, on ground henceforth to be called
the Shaftesbury Park Estate. Glancing at
the list of shareholders in this company, or-
ganised, of course, on the "limited" system,
we find more than a hundred leading names,
any of which would be a stamp of authenticity
on an undertaking so humane and economical
as the work at Lavender-bill, Wandsworth.
A diversity which might almost be called
picturesque appears in this notable cata-
logue. Shoulder to shoulder in the good work
are the Bishops of Chester, Carlisle, Salisbury,
and Winchester ; Dr. Manning and Mr.
Tupper; Sir John Pakington, Mr. Thomas
Hughes, and Mr. Carlyle; Mr. Thomas
Brassey and Mr. Alfred Tennyson, Mr. Dar-
win and the Duke of Norfolk; Mr. Ruskin
and Mr. Samuel Morley; Sir Charles Wheat
stone and the Marquis Townsend; in brief,
the representatives of all imaginable forms and
shades of thought and opinion united upon
one point—the lore of mankind.
The estate on which Mr. Robert Austin, the
company's architect, will erect houses of old
English design adapted. to modern require-
ments, and sufficiently varied to avoid the
monotonous pattern too often allowed to
mar an extensive building plan, includes about
forty acres and is situate midway between
Battersea acres,
and Clapham Common. Three
classes of dwellings, all being separate houses
of one storey, are designed to accommodate
families differing in their need of room; and
the number of these buildings in all will be
upwards of 1,200. Co-operative stores, schools
and class-rooms, a concert and lecture hall,
library, reading-rooms, workmen's club, baths,
and a gymnasium are all amply provided for;
and there will be left three acres at least of
garden ground for the healthful recreation of
the " citizens " great and small. The open
spot will be somewhere near the centre, as the
architect's plan denotes, and an orchard whioh
now forms part of the building site is to be
obliterated. This, we suppose, cannot be
helped, as it would be a good thing to have
pear, trees bearing in the very midst of a well'
ordered population, just to show how far the
youth of the English working class has ad-
vanced beyond orchard-robbing. The ceremony
of laying the memorial stone, on which was
graven the motto "Happy Homes; the best
condition of Social Progress," was performed,
as already intimated, by the Earl of Shaftes-
bury, Mr. Walton, as chairman of the com-
pany, presiding. Letters were read from Lord
Derby, Sir Walter Trevelyan, Sir Richard
Wallace, and several other friends and sub-
scribers of the enterprise, excusing their per-
sonal attendance; and, after the eloquent and
hopeful speech of Lard Shaftesbury, Mr.
Chadwick moved, and Mr. Taylor seconded, a
vote of thanks to his lordship.
Refreshments were served in a tent on the
ground.

THE WEEK'S NEWS.

The report of the Select Committee on
Railway Amalgamation was issued on Monday.
It recommends that all amalgamation Bills
should be referred to a permanent and spe-
cially selected joint committee.

A charge of arson against a licensed vic-
tualler was investigated at the Clerkenwell
Police-court on Tuesday, when Thomas Wil
Barn Walton was accused of having set fire to
the Britannia public-house, Gray's-inn-road,
his wife and two children being inmates of
the place at the time. Some evidence for the
prosecution having been taken, the prisoner
was remanded, without bail.

The suspicion respecting the truth of the
story told by the woman Morris, which ma
that she had thrown into the water at Rich-
mond a young man named Frank Martin,
turns out to have been well founded. She has
been again brought before the local magis-
trates, charged upon her own confession with
Martin's murder, but not the slightest evi-
donee could be brought forward in support of
her statement, and she was discharged.

A dock labourer named,Green:wason Tuesday
charged, at the Thames Police-court with the
murder of .his wife. The crime had followed a
night's drinking at a neighbouring public-
house. Evidence was given that the prisoner
and the deceased were "nearly always quar-
relling." A remand was granted.

Mr. Gladstone, in answer to the represen-
tation of the Wesleyan Conference on the illl-
- of continuing the Contagious Diseases
Acts, stated that the subject should receive
his full consideration, and that when it was
again before the Government he would be
glad to communicate personally with the
members of the Conference.

The opening of a new pier at Hastings on
Monday was made the occasion of some local
rejoicing. The ceremony was performed by
Lord Granville, and at the complimentary
breakfast which was given, Mr. Brassey,
M.P., presided.

Nearly 43,000 persons visited the Bethnal-
green Museum last week. The total number
admitted since the opening of the institution
has been 320,833.

The eighth annual meeting of the National
Artillery Assoeiation was opened at Shoebury-
nen on Monday.

The Regattas of the South Eastern Coast
were inaugurated at Dover on Monday. Prince
Arthur and Earl Granville were amongst the
visitors, and there were a large • nuw ber of
pleasure-seekers from the imniediato neighbour-
hood.

Although the French Government has not
yet been able to fix the precise reduction to be
made from the subscriptions so lavishly made
to the New Loan, it has so far approached the
real value Of the subscription, that it has
officially fixed at not less than 71 nor more
than 8 per cent. the proportion to be granted
to each subsoribtar. This, taking it at the
lowest estimate, is a distinct declaration that
the subscription covered the Loan at least ten
times.

A telegraphic despatch, from a correspon-
dent at Alexandria, states that an Egyptian
army of 2,000 men with a reserve of 3,000
more had advanced into Abysinnia with a view'
to conquering the country. The Emperor
Kassai was marching against them with a
superior Throe in point of numbers, but it was
believed that, as the Egyptians were provided
with Remington rifles and mitrailleuses, the
Abyssinians would be defeated and Magdala
eventually taken. Some European adven-
turers t!re said to accompany the invading
force.

On his way to the watering-place of Gastein,
made famous by the resort of crowned headF,
the Emperor of Germany was received at
Weis by the Archduke Karl Ludwig, who
'welcomed him in the name of the Emperor
Fermis Joseph, and accompanied him on his
Journey to Salzburg. After visiting his son,
the Crown Prince, at Berchtesgaden, the
Emperor William proceeded to Gastein.

M. Tillers, aceorapanied by his family, loft
Paris on Monday moriiing for Trouville. He
is said to be in excellent health.

tried the other day before the Assize Court of
Versailles, M. Jules Favre was retained for

With regard to the visit of the English
Volunteers to Belgium next month, sanction
for which has been given by the Secretary for
War, a meeting of the Council of the Anglo-
Belgian Prize Fund was held, and a numerous
committee was appointed to co-operate with
the council. It was announced that very nu-
merous applications from all parts of the
Kingdom were coming in; and a deputation
was appointed to proceed at once to Belgium,
and ascertain what arrangements had been
made on this side for the event. •

Tho Crown Princess of Denmark has given
birth to a son.

For picking pockets at the wedding of
Mdlle. Nilsson, two lads have been sentenced:to
prison for ton days and reformatory for five
years.

At Clerkenwell Police Court a charge of
falsely using the •title of surgeon was ad-
journed for a week—the medical man who
prosecuted stating that, in a particular case,
the defendant had certified the cause of death
to be "want of breath."

King Amadeo has been very warmly received
by the population at San Sebastian. While
detained at Santander by bad weather, he went
on board the mail steamer Chimborazo, which
touched there on her way to Lisbon and South
America. llis Majesty spent several hours in
examining the vessel, took lunch with the
passengers, and on his departure, as on his
arrival, was greeted with hearty British
cheers.

The Faculty of Political Economy in the
University at Munich has conferred the degree
of Doctor upon Mr. Gladstone, Mr. John
Stuart Mill, and the Earl of Shaftesbury.

It is announced from Cairo that the Khedive
has returned to Egypt from his recent visit to
the Sultan at Constantinople,

There is said to be great rejoicing among
the American Democrats at the success of their
oandidato in North Carolina, but the
Republicans maintain that the complete
returns will show that their party has been
victorious.

The Wesleyan Conference has adopted a re-
solution expressive of sympathy with the
policy of Prince Bismarck in respect to the
treatment of the Jesuits in Germany.

An action for slander and libel, in which
both the plaintiff and the defendant were
clergymen, was tried at Saturdays sitting of
the Guildford Assizes. The Rev. Mr. Mao-
donnell, lately curate of Lower Norwood,
claimed £2,000 from the Rev. J. E. Kempe,
rector of St. James's, Piccadilly, as compensa-
tion for the loss of clerical employment, caused
through Mr. Kempe's action in consequence of
the plaintiff's having performed a marriage
ceremony, in which the lady had been divorced
from her former husband on the ground of
adultery. The jury returned a verdict for the
defendant.

Three cases in which cabmen were the de-
fendants came before 'metropolitan .-police
courts on Saturday. At Bow-street George
James was fined in a small penalty for leaving
his vehicle unattended. At Marlborough-
street Abraham Elliott was fined 30s. and
12s. 6d: costs for having cruelly treated his
horse. The principal facts were deposed to by
Sir 'Henry heave, M.P. At Westminster
James Holford was summoned for furious
driving and running over a child eight years
of age. The case was adjourned in order that
the defendant might have an opportunity of
compensating the child's parents.

1 A curious strike was lately declared at a
large hotel at A.rnheim, in Holland. Some 70
or 80 persons were in the habit of db.ing
there daily, and the guests were about to place
themselves at the table, when the waiters all
threw down their napkins and marched out of
the place. Great anxiety was experienced for
a moment as to how all the eager stomachs
were to be satisfied, but the proprietor called
to his aid his family and the falai() servants
of the establishment, and the dinner passed
off well.

An Irish labourer named Patrick Malone,
living at Leeds, was taken into custody on
Wednesday morning on the charge of having
murdered his wile, whom he had kicked to
death,

A. vein of goli ore is reported to have been
discovered in a btone quarry atilallinspittle,
near ,liinsale. The police are guarding the
quarry, where work has been ftuspended for
home tune.

Autumn congresses have commenced. The
archteologists opened theirs on Monday at
Wolverhampton, under the pri sideuey of the
Earl of Dartmouth, who took occasion to
vindicate the men of the Blftek Country
against popular disparagement of thoir morals
and intolligenoe,

The man Taylor, who murdered a woman
and child at Bermondsey a short time since,
has changed for the worst. On Monday he
became so violent that he had to be bound
down in bed. Little or no hope of his
recovery is now entertained.

It is announced that Colonel Amcotts the
present Liberal member for Mid-Lincolnlire,
proposes to retire from the representation of
that constituency at the dissolution..

A great meeting was held in the Free Trade
Hall, Manchester, on Tuesday evening, in
favour of Home Goverment for Ireland. Sir
George Bowyer, M.P. presided, and the chief
speakers were Mr. M.P.,
M.P. Professor
Galbraith, Dublin, and Mr. A. M. Sullivan.
Resolutions in favour of Home Rule, and
pledging Irishmen to support none but Home
Rule candidates were passed.

Notice of further advance in the price of
coil was given on Wednesday morning
by several leading colliery firms in South
orkshire. The price of house coal is now
20s. per ton at Sheffield. Twel#e months ago
it could be had for 9s. Slack coal is advanced
to 12s. Gd., two years since it realised 53. It
will be remembered that the last advance of
coal took place on August Ist. These continued
rises are occasioning great anxiety to iron
masters and steel manufacturers.

A shocking accident occurred early on Wed-
nesday morning, near Barnsley, in sinking a
shaft at Wentworth Colliery, Stanbro'. John
Kelly, the foreman sinker, and four other men,
descended the shaft. Kelly began to drill out
a shot which had been lighted on the previous
night, when the charge exploded, killing him
and seriously injuring two other men, one of
whom lies in a precarious state.

In the House of Lords in the discussion
upon the Military Forces Localization Bill, the
Marquis of Salisbury declared his satisfaction
that nothing was to be done toward establish-
ing a military centre at Oxford, till the
University authorities had had an opportunity
of expressing their opinion.

In the House of Commons on Monday Mr.
Cardwell stated, in reply to a question about
a volunteer who had been dismissed from his
regiment for presiding at a Republican meet-
ing, that the colonel had statutory power to
dismiss.

In the New Licensing Bills grocers who
hold spirit licences are to be placed on the
same footing as publicans.

A facsimile of a letter purporting to have
been written by Prince Bismarck to his wife
two days after the battle of Sedan has been
published, in the Paris Figaro.

Lisbon has experienced an alarm of con-
spiracy, but the plot was discovered in time
by the police, and full disclosures are promised.
The population is loyally indignant against
the foiled conspirators, and order prevails
throughout the kingdom.

One of the cyclones which' periodically sweep
across the Bay of Bengal has committed de
vastation among the local shipping. The
Omaha, of Liverpool, was driven ashore on
Saugor Buffs, not far from Calcutta. All the
light-ships in the Hoogbley were carried away,
and the station of BalaSore, over :which the
storm broke with great fury, has been entirely
wrecked,

The Lambeth Waterworks Company have
successfully opened the new intake from the
Thames at 'West Moulsey, by which water of
a purer and fresher quality will be conveyed
to Thames Litton, for distribution thence over
the immense area supplied on the south side
of the river. This is a great 814 in advance,
and will tend to obviate the possibility of a
"water famine" amongst the trauspontine
residents, numbering several hundreds of
thousands, dependent on the company.

The wife of Mr. James Milborne, grocer, of
Frome, presented her husband with three
infant children on Monday night last. Mother
and children are doing well.

Liverpool aspires to be the first of the great
boroughs to ba its house in order for the
Ballot. A schotuo is being devised to divide
it into polliug districts.

A salmon cobble from Berwick-upon•Tweod,
containing seven men, was overset, and six of
its occupants instautly drowned. The seventh
contrived to cling to an our, and was happily
rescued.

The works whieh were commenced last year
for extending the line of communication from
Blackfriars Bridge to Chelsea, by means of an
embankment from the grounds of Chelsea
Hospital to a point near the Middlesex side of
Battersea Bridge, are now fast approaching,
completion, seven hundred feet of the new
granite wall having recen4 been exposed to
yiow by Oa remoyal ef the piles,

According to advioes received in Paris the
Garonne and other rivers in the South of
France have overflowed.

A Paris correspondent contradicts the re-
port that the Due d'Aumale intends to retire
from public life in consequence of the death
of his son the Duo do Guise.

There was a prosecution at the Thames
Police-court on Saturday for the illegal storage
of gunpowder. The defendant, Henry Nathan
by name, was charged with having 250 lb&
of this dangerous material in his possession
within three miles of the City, contrary to
the statute. He was fined £lO, and the
gunpowder was ordered to he forfeited.

On Saturday the French Assembly watt
closed by M. Grevy, the President, and it
will not re•open until the llth. of next
November. M. Thiers has proceeded to
Trouville, but will return to Versailles once
a week, in order, to preside over ,a Council of
Ministers. While at TrouVille M. Thiers will
grant no audiences whatever, except to private
friends, it being his desire to enjoy complete
repose during his holiday.

From Rome we learn that although the
Clerical party mustered in good force its can-
didates were completely beaten by the Liberals
at the elections on Sunday. This result is re-
garded as all the more important, because the
Pope is said to have felt confident of victory,
and counted on being able to prove to the
world that the population of Rome was really
in his fayour.

Mr. Gladstone, aceompanied,by his son, tho
meinber for Whitby, left town on Saturdoy
for Ilawarden Castle.

'Another fatal railway accident; this
time resulting in the loss of either fuur or
six lives, and serious injuries to many, pas-
sengers, is reported from the neighbourhood
of Manchester. An express train was travel-
ling on the Laneashire ,and l'orkshite Rail-
way, when a coal trdin ran out of a siding,
and, a collision taking place between the two
engines, Serious loss of life and property
ensued. The driver of the oollier train avers
that the signals
,were in his favour, but this
will doubtless be inquired into at the inquest.

A young woman, named Fanny. Taylor, a
domestio servant, committed suicide at King-
ston-on,Thaines on Wednesday. She was at
her situation the previous night, but bad seen
the young man with whom she was keeping
company walking out with another woman.
This seems to have preyed upon her mind, and
she drowned herself in the Hog's Mill river.
The act was discovered by is woman, who
found the deceased's jacket and bonnet on the
bank of the stream.

Cholera is reported to be prevalent on (ho
Looshai frontier, and a few eases havo
occurred in the neighbourhood of Calcutta.

At Sanger, in the central provinces, a
groundless panto, occasioned by fears of a
mutiny among the 40th Madras Native
Infantry, led to the removal of all women and
children, from the station. When every pre-
caution had been taken against a rising, it
was ascertained that none had ever been
intended.-

Mr. Butt, it is said, has been Specially
retained. for the defence of the Bishop of
Olonfort in the Galway election proseoution.

Lord Westbury has appointed Messrs.
Mercer and Mercer solicitors, and Messrs.
Young and Price, official liquidators,' under
the European Arbitration Act. Business has
been discontinued at the company's offices in
Waterloo-place. , _

William Lace, charged with brutally mur-
dering his wife by kicking her to death, WaS
tried at Bristol, before Mr. Justice Atelier, and
sentenced to death.

An original and audacious form of robbery
has been practised on the London, Brighton,
and South Coast Railway Company. A woman
was detected carrying off three curtains and
a carpet from a tirst-class carriage on their
line, and when arrested soveu tirst-class
tiokuts were found upon her.

Small-pox has broken out at Cinderford, in
the Lean _Forest, iu a virulent form, and some
tatal cases have been reported.

A return of the revenue of the Corporation
of Melbourne siaco tho year 1667 has been,
published, which clearly demonstrates the
increase of the wealth and population of the
.capital of Victoria. In 1807 tne city revenue
was, in round numbers, £73,000;' in .1868;.
4:71 000 ; 18 in ; 1870
• I
X 86,000; and in "71 1,000.

Vice-Chancellor is to be t'w "vaca-
tion judge" ill eilanaery ; Mr. Juetice Quarini
tilo nioit recently- appointed) ie the " YlkO4t,
tion judge " clullubva, -

Captain King Harman, the Home Ruler,
has formally withdrawn from the Home Rule
Association in consequence of its having, as
he says, permitted its platform to be made a
means and a stepping-stone to enable worthless
persons to elbow themselves into the House of
Parliament, place, and emolument, and by
their base conduct to bring disgrace on what
ought to be a most respectable community.
Be speaks of Judge Keogh as a firm, brave,
and high-spirited gentleman, and deprecates
the abuse heaped on him by an ill-governed,
misdirected people.

Accounts from the Black Sea state that
supplies of wheat from there would have been
impossible this year, even if the magnificent
crop.' in France had not rendered them
needless,

Count Beust, after a long stay at Vienna,
where he o t Count Andrassy on his return
from his estate at Terebes, has proceeded to
his country . seat, Altenberg Castle, near
Griefenstein, on the Danube. He will thence
go to Gastein to take the waters, and at the
end of September, before returning to London,
make another visit to Vienna.

At the Manchester Assizes, on Tuesday, a
dressmaker, named Pendlebury, obtained a
verdict for £450 for breach M promise by a
farmer named Ectoek, living near llorwich.

M. Worms, Professor of the Faculty of Law
at Rennes, has been designated by the French
Government to represent it at the Interna-
tional Statistical Congress which is shortly to
open at St. Petersburg.

Mr. C. E. Lewis, solicitor, of London, has
00018 forward as a Conservative candidate for
the city of Londonderry. He declares himself
in favonr, of the purchase of the Irish railways
by Ow state, and of national as opposed to
denominational education.

On Wednesday much interest was evinced
at the Bow-street Pollee-court by a large
number of persons who had collected to hear
the proceedings in the cash of Mr. Anicljah,.a
cigar merchant, against Mr. Onslow, M.P.,
and Mr. Whalley, M.P., for the recovery
of some document connected with "the
Claimant's" meetings, which are being held at
various places. The summons was eventually
diSniSssed, after an miting hearing.

On Tuesday at the Leeds Police-court, a
man named Rhodes was charged with poaching
and assaults in Rounding Park, The prisoner
aud another man not in custody were caught
poaching by a policeman and an assistant on
Thursday night last, and they attacked and
severely beat the policeman and his companion,
who, however, managed to capture the prisoner.
He was sentenced to various terms of im-
prisonment for the several offences, amounting
to ten months in all, and was also bound over
to be of good behaviour for two years after-
wards.

The mortality in London and twenty otter
large towns of the United Kingdom was at the
rate last week of 27 deaths annually to every
1,000 persons estimated to be living. In the
metropolis 2,252 births and 1,693 deaths were
registered, the former having exceeded by 39
the average number, while the deaths were 65
below it, Twenty-eight persons died from
small-pox, 20 from measles, 6 from scarlet
fever, 6 ftom diphtheria, 49 from whooping-
cough, 28 from different forms of fever (of
which 4 were certified as typhus, 17 as enteric
or typhoid, and 7 as simple continued fever),
and 484 from diarrheea. The fatal cases of
whooping-cough continue excessive, but the
deaths referred to each of the other prineipal
zymotic diseases were below the corrected
average.

Committal to the Central Criminal Court
at the charge of wilful murder was the result
of the renewed examination at the Mansion
House of Frank Fisher, who killed a fellow-
workman in Laurence Pountney-laue on the
20th July.

At Guikihall Police-court, William Cart-
wright was accused of obtaining by false
pretences, from a person in Gloucester who
had advertised the instrument for sale, ft
fiddle, worth £25 ; and tho prisoner, whose
intercepted correspondence showed that he
made a practice of answering similar adver-
tisements, was remanded, there being several
charges against him.

Sir James RamsaY, of Baniff, having agreed
to let his house, lands, and moors for the
coming season to one gentleman, ()hanged his
mind about the deeirability of his tenant, and
relet his property to another person. The
original lessee holds to his bond, and Vice-
Chancellor Malin has declared that the lessor
could not be permitted to break hia agreement
and lease the property co—another, and has
granted an. injunction to prevent any other
parsen than the plaintiff—the first lessee—
killing game or using dogs on the lands of
Bare during A.ugutit and Beptembar.

A. movement has been started for the
purpose of presenting a testimonial to Mr.
George Smith, of Coalville, near Leicester,
who has laboured to ameliorate the condition
of the women and children employed in brick-
fields.

According to the Poor-law returns, the
total number of paupers in the metropolitan
district last week was 101,495, of whom
31,763 were in workhouses and 69,732 received
out-door relief. Compared with the corres-
ponding weeks in 1871, 1870, and 1869, these
figures show a decrease of 18,070, 25,833, and
23,460 respectively. The number of vagrants
relieved was 495.

Another advauce in the prices of certain
descriptions of finished iron is reported from
Wolverhampton.

On Wednesday an inquiry was held by Mr.
Humphreys, the Middlesex coroner, respecting
the death of James Barrett, aged 32, a dock
labourer, who was killed in a brawl in a
public-house in North Woolwich, on the 26th
July. After hearing the evidence, the. jury
returned a verdict of manslaughter against a
man named Thomas Spring, who was proved
to have struck the deceased.

At Belper, near Chesterfield, on Wednesday,
two young men named Green and Thompson
were remanded on the charge of brutally
murdering a female tramp named Hopkinson,
whose body was found on the highway in a
shocking state, there being indications that
she had been dreadfully maltreated and jumped
upon. Prisoners say that the women was
killed by lightning while in their comyany.

The Association Generale d'Alsace•Lorraine
has given notice to the inhabitants or the
districts lately conceded to the Germans, that
on the 30th September the option of making
a declaration that they are French citizens
will cease, and calls upon them to take the
necessary steps without loss of time to take
rank for themselves and children as French
subjects.

in the House of Commons on Wednesday,
the Licensing Bill, after long discussion:was
read a third time amid cheers, Sir Wilfrid
Lawson having previously stated that he did
not mean to divide the House.

In recognition of the services of Mr. Chi
cheater Fortesoue as Chief Secretary for Ire-
land, a deputation consisting of a large
number of noblemen and gentlemen waited
upon the Countess Waldegrave, and preiented
to her ladyship the portrait of her husband.
Mr. Chichester Fortescue acknowledged the
gift in a well-chosen speech.

Sir Henry Rawlinson has, made a handsome
amende to Mr. Stanley, in a letter 1 thanking
intelligence
from for being the bearer of direct
from Dr. Livingstone to several members of
the Council of the Royal Geographical Society,
and tendering" most cordial acknowledgments
for the timely succour rendered to Dr. Living-
stone in his great need," and an expression of
the "energy, perseverance, and courage" with
which the American searcher conducted his
expedition.

An action, brought by Mr. Leonard
Edmunds, late clerk of the Patents, against
the publisher of TheY Daily Telegraph, to
recover damages for an alleged libel in the
issue of the 18th 'January, 1870, was tried
before Mr. Baron Martin and a special jury, at
the Guildford Assizes, and resulted in a verdict
for the defendant. The libel was said to be
contained in an abbreviated report of a
Treasury minute, which stated that the
plaintiff after his accounts had been investi-
gated, was indebted largely, to the Crown for
fees received by virtue of his office, and not
paid over according to law. Mr. Gladstone,
Mr. Lowe, and Mr. Stansfeld were present to
give evidence for the defendant, but were not
called. Similar actions against the publishers
of the Daily News and. Bela, were with-
drawn.

After a few days of comparatively quiescent
and cool. weather, London was again visited on
Wednesday with sultry heat and thunder-
storms, the latter being in some districts very
intense, and everywhere accompanied by heavy
rainfall. Woolwich and Greenwich, and the
places there adjacent, seem to have.suffered
most; the rain fell in a perfect deluge, many
buildings were flooded, *end the shell foundry
in the Royal Arsenal was eighteen inches
under water. Beverat bifildings were struck
and damaged by the lightning; and fatal
results to human life are apprehended.

Handling the subject of the meeting of the
three Emperors at Berlin, the Prorinzial
Correspondenz bids nobody feel any alarm at
the unusual gathering together of the Eagles,
for "the preservation of the _
'peace in Europe
is the object of the three Monarchs," and
aseribes to the attitude of Germany the merit
of having smoothed the way to a raoroolte-
me lit between Austria ana Russia.

The strike at Milan still continues, and
some arrests have been made. The city, how-
ever, is quiets

The Moniteur Beige publishes a decree of
the Minister of the Interior, dated the 6th
inst., prohibiting the import of cattle coming
from Germany and the north of Russia.

The Lords Commissioners of the Admiralty
are expected at Plymouth on Monday next to
make their annual inspection of thb dockyards
and the other naval establishments at that
port.

The Royal Agricultural Society of Ireland
and the North-East Agricultural Association
opened their joint show on Wednesday at
Oymeau-paik, Belfast. Among their visitors
were the Lord Lieutenant and the Countess
Spencer, and Lord and Lady Lurgan. The
show was in every respect successful.

The Committee of Fortifications are now
examining Gravelines, Dunkirk, Lille, and
Calais, which will be fortified so as to render
them an impregnable, square ,of fortresses for
defending the North of France.

The complete result of the elections for the
Efungarian Chamber of Deputies is now known.
The Ministerial candidates gained the day in
246 districts, and those of the Opposition in
146.

The mercantile clerks of 'Liverpool held a
numerous meeting 'on Wednesday night, at
which a memorial was adopted urging upon
the employers the necessity of augmenting the
salaries of clerks, as business had largely in-
creased, and a general advance had been made
in almost every other department of the labour
market. The meeting was adjourned for a
month to report progress. One clerk stated
that a friendly society in Liverpool, which
employed between fifty and sixty clerks, many
of them married, paid salaries not exceeding
from 15s. to 20s. per week.

H.E.H. the Duke, of Edinburgh arrived at
Dover on Thursday morning, by special
steamer, the Maid of Kent, Caption Pittock,
from Calais. The Duke was received by Major-
General Sir Alfred Horsford and his staff, and,
after a short interview, his Royal Highness
left by mail train of the South Eastern Rail-
way for London.

In consequence of the lamented death of
the last scion of the D'Aumale (Albemarle)
House, the Imperial Court of Austria will go
into mourning for sixteen days from the 6th
of August.

A delegate meeting was held on Wednesday
evening at the Arundel Club, Arundel-street,
to consider the propositions which have been
put forward by l‘lr. Samuel Morley, M.P.
The meeting was strictly private, none being
admitted save the delegates of political socie-
ties. Each society numbering 100 members
or upwards was permitted to send two dele-
gates, one delegate only being admitted from a
society consisting of less than 100 members.

The Princess Louise and the Marquis of
Lorne arrived at Ardrishaig on Tuesday, and
landed on the quay. A royal salute was fired
from the Lochgilphead battery by three gun
detachments of the 10th Argyle, under com-
mand of Captain MachLachlan. The Princess
and Lady Elizabeth Campbell drove to Culbon
Mhor, the seat of Mr. John Malcolm, and re-
turned to Auchindarroeh at four, whilst the
Marquis remained to superintend the heavy
gun competition. The Prineess afterwards
went to see the contest.

Lord Lyons has been informed by the
French Minister for Foreign Affairs, that
special instructions have been sent to the
police agents on the Franco-Swiss and Franco
-
Italian frontiers, to allow British subjects to
enter and quit France witllont passports.

The mallet with which Sir Christopher
Wren laid the foundation-stone of St. Paul's
Cathedral, on J 11716 21, 1675, will be used by
the Princess Teeh. next Wednesday, when her
Royal Highness will perform a similar office
for the new Church Schools at Kingston.

The ship Friends' Adventure, from Port
Ballintory to Port Dunda, ha e been wrecked
on Rathha Island. Crew saved.

In the Roll Chambers application was made
in the case of " Gladstone v. the Duke of New-
castle" for permission to sell the house in which
his Grace had resided in Cat lton House-terrace,
by private contract, for £45,000. It was
proved that this sum was the full value of the
building, and an order for the conditional sale
was made.

Three girls whose ages varied from 13 to
18, were on Wednesday charged at Marylebone
Poliee-eourt wsth having' been guilty of dis-
orderly conduct ia dressing themselves as
sailors. It was explained to the magistrate
that the whole affair whs a Joke, and the
defendants were accordingly discharged.

FRIDAY.
Another advance in the prices of certain
descriptions of finished iron is reported. from
Wolverhampton.
Mr. James Vinson, of 35, Langton-street,
Cathay, committed suicide by throwing himself
from Clifton Suspension Bridge on Tuesday,
night. He fell upon the road, and was killed
instantly.

The combined Channel and Reserve Squadrons,
numbering fifteen ships, are to be in Plymouth
Sound on the 16th inst., and in Torbay on the

17th inst.

At the meeting of the Rotherham Town
Council, on Wednesday it was stated that
another considerable advance in the price of
coal would be made yesterday, and the price
for lighting the public lamps was raised from
458. to 555. per lamp for 2,600 hours' lighting
Yesterday twelve English gentlemen and
players sailed from Liverpool for Canada, in the
Sarmatian, Allan Line, with the view of
playing exhibition cricket matches in Canada,
and probably in the States.
Tne number of messages forwarded from
postal telegraph stations during last week was
330,590, showing an increase of 77,455
messages.
The sittings of the court-martial upon
Marshal Bazaine have been re-opened, and
General Changarnier's testimony was taken.

The Stockholm steamer (Ekdahl), from
Newport. with rails, was aground on Wednes-
day in Helsingfors harbour, and ,was leaking
Considerably. The G. F. Gibbon (McLaughlin),
of and from London to Troon, in ballast,
foundered on 31st July; the crew have bt;en
landed at Liverpool.
Between twelve and. one o'clouk yesterday
morning a fire broke out in the rooms of Mr.
Charles M'Carthy, a lodger in the house,
No. 36, Luke-street, Mile-end New Town.
M'Cartby, who is about 4-0 years of age, was
severely burned. His wife was also injured
by the flames, and both of them were removed
to a hospital.
A telegram from Kingston,. Jamaica, dated
4th inst., says :—lmpoi taut fire. in Port Royal-
street, at the stores and premises of Messrs.
A. L. Malabre and Co., and George Solomons
and Co.; fire extinguished most providen-
tially; no other damage."

The severe thunderstorm has caused much
damage in the Staffordshire-Potteries. A part
of the Newcastle branch of the North Stafford-
shire Railway has been washed away; and the
main line for a considerable distance hait
become submerged.

The deputy-coroner for East Middlesex held
an inquiry yesterday at Hackney into the
death of Sarah Chandler, aged 49, of 2,
Homerton-terrace, Hackney, who committed
suicide on Sunday by taking a quantity of
"Battle's Vermin Powder." She frequently
complained of the pains in her head. On
Sunday, while sitting at dinner, deceased
suddenly said, "I can do nothing, my head is
so bad. lam afraid my brain is giving way."
The jury returned a verdict of " Suicide
whilst of unsoand mind."

A large meeting of the creditors of Edward
Vigers, of Harrow-road, bucf,ter, was held at
the Cannon-street Hotel yesterday, when Mr.

Sydney Smith, the receiver of the firm of
Sydney Smith, Harvey, and Co., 65, Basing-
hall-street, public accountants, submitted a
statement of the affairs, which showed a sur-
plus of £44,000 after paying 20s. in the
pound. The proposal to pay 20s. in the
pound, together with 5 per cent. interest, in
fbur instalments of ss. each, the first instal-
ment payable in June, 1675, and the ra't
minder in the three following months, wigi
accepted almost unanimously, and a nom-
mitte.e of five creditors was chosen, with 11r.
Sydney Smith to see the terms ot the offer
were carried out.

Referring, to the report of Mrs. Oladstone's
Convalescent nom, Mr. Freeman, of llud.
derstield, writes that at Meltham, near that
town, a convalescent home erected. by the late
Mr. Charles Brook for the poor of the district
at the cost of i 50,000, is perfectly free, and
that during the past year 425 patients hitN.+6
been received.

near the Sheffield station to the fast trio
leaving London at five o'clock in the afternoon.

station, and as the train was passing over
some points, the engine ran along one line,
